false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() stops terminating remaining flusher processes after the deadline expires

join() sets the shared stopped flag and then iterates over all flusher processes, but if waiting for an early process consumes the deadline, the `break` at lines 339-341 exits the loop before terminate() is attempted for every later process. Those daemon flusher processes can therefore keep polling Redis and producing segments after the strategy has supposedly joined, including after a rebalance or shutdown, and can compete with a replacement flusher for the same shards. All processes should be terminated even when the waiting deadline has already expired.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid flusher process counts are not rejected and can disable flushing

The CLI accepts any integer for --flusher-processes and SpanFlusher performs no validation. A negative value makes num_processes negative at line 60, producing an empty process_to_shards_map and spawning no flusher at all, while submit() finds no backpressure values and continues accepting spans into Redis indefinitely. A value of 0 passed programmatically is also silently changed by `max_processes or len(...)` into one process per shard instead of being rejected or honored. The process count should be validated as >= 1 at the CLI/factory/flusher boundary.

Multi-process flusher test never verifies that shared-process shards actually flush

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the number of processes and that four shard ids appear in process_to_shards_map; it submits no spans and asserts no produced segment for any shard. A regression in the shard-subset SpansBuffer construction, the new SpanFlusher.main() argument order, or flushing when multiple shards share one process/thread would therefore still pass. The test should push spans for shards handled by both processes and assert the flushed output.

Restarting a hung threaded flusher creates a duplicate flusher for the same shards

When produce_to_pipe is used, flushers are threading.Thread objects. _ensure_processes_alive() detects a hang, but the kill at lines 253-257 is skipped because a thread is not a multiprocessing.Process, and _create_process_for_shards() then starts a second thread for the same shards while the hung thread may later resume. Both threads can call flush_segments(), produce the same segment, and call done_flush_segments() for the same shards, risking duplicate buffered segments. Overwriting self.processes[process_index] also loses the only handle to the old thread, so join() can no longer wait for or stop it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Close stops committing before queued work is drained

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, and it never waits for queues to empty. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so a worker that finishes its current item exits at the loop condition instead of draining remaining queued items. Consequently queued items are abandoned on graceful shutdown and any items workers do finish after the commit thread stops never have their offsets committed, causing avoidable duplicate reprocessing and violating the graceful-shutdown expectation.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore commit past a message whose processing failed, so it will never be retried or sent to a DLQ. This directly contradicts the strategy docstring claiming it only commits offsets after successful processing and can silently lose uptime results.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() on a string group key. For strings, hash() is randomized per interpreter process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the same subscription maps to different queues in different processes and across restarts. That breaks the documented consistent-assignment/ordering guarantee whenever work for a group moves between consumer processes or the consumer restarts, and makes distribution non-reproducible; a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5, as used elsewhere in the uptime consumer) should be used instead.

Shared queue pool is destroyed by the first strategy close and reused after rebalance

The FixedQueuePool (and its worker threads and OffsetTracker) is created once on the factory and handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo creates/closes strategies on partition assignment and rebalance; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down that shared pool, and queue.Queue.put() on a shut-down queue raises ShutDown. The next assignment reuses the same dead pool (factory only nulls it in factory.shutdown(), not on strategy close), so subsequent messages fail to enqueue, are swallowed by submit()'s broad except handler, and are marked complete without processing. The shared OffsetTracker also retains last_committed across assignments, so a partition reassigned at a lower offset can never be committed again.

Submit swallows grouping/decoder failures and marks the offset complete

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one broad except that logs the error and then add_offset()+complete_offset()s the message. Any failure in grouping_fn (or an enqueue failure such as a shut-down queue) therefore makes the message eligible for offset commit even though it was never processed, silently dropping it instead of surfacing the failure to Arroyo for retry/DLQ handling.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected when workers fall behind. Arroyo will keep submitting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them, accumulating decoded WorkItems (including the original Kafka message) in memory indefinitely, growing OffsetTracker sets for uncommittable partitions as well. A slow subscription or downstream outage therefore risks OOM and massive reprocessing on restart rather than natural backpressure as claimed in the class docstring.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' without escaping or length-prefixing. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct triples produce the same key: for example name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both produce "..._dashboards:read_a_b_c". A denial for one resource can consequently fast-path-deny a different resource for 30 seconds. Use an unambiguous encoding such as separated, escaped, or hashed components.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache key omits identity type and can poison renderer checks

The denial key is built only from namespace, raw subject UID, action, name, and parent folder, ignoring checkReq.IdentityType. Anonymous subjects and the render service both commonly use UID "0"; an anonymous denial for dashboards:read on a dashboard is therefore cached under the same key as a render-service check for that dashboard. The later render check returns Allowed:false from permDenialCache before getRendererPermissions can return its wildcard read permission, incorrectly breaking rendering for up to the 30-second denial TTL. Include the identity type (or do not denial-cache synthetic identities such as renderer) in the key.

Denials caused by the stale folder tree are cached, extending folder staleness

On a cached-permission miss Check re-queries permissions from the DB, but checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions still resolve ancestors through buildFolderTree, which returns the short-TTL cached folder tree without refreshing it. For a dashboard whose access is inherited from an ancestor above its immediate parent, a newly created/re-parented folder can therefore still produce Allowed:false, and lines 153-155 then write that result into permDenialCache. The false denial is now pinned for another denial-cache TTL even after the folder tree refreshes, partially defeating the PR's goal for newly created folders. Do not denial-cache denials that depended on the folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the DB fallback path.

Every denied check for a new resource name bypasses the permission cache to the DB

If cached permissions do not allow the requested name, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which after this PR always queries the permission store. The denial cache only helps repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent); a caller probing or enumerating many distinct dashboard/folder names—each a distinct denial key—forces a full permission DB query per name, with singleflight only deduplicating concurrent identical requests. This removes the previous cache protection against sequential negative-check DB load and needs a bound (for example revalidate at most once per cached permission-set generation/TTL window) rather than per-resource requery.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered list is rendered without a React key

The 'grafana' branch returns <GrafanaRuleListItem> without `key={key}`, unlike the 'datasource' branch on line 165 and the Unknown branch on line 168 which both pass key. FilterView builds a deduplicated artificial key via getRuleKey for exactly this purpose. Without it React warns and, more importantly, may reuse component instances (including RuleActionsButtons state such as silence drawer/delete modal/redirect state) for different rules when the infinite-scroll list appends or reorders, showing actions for the wrong rule.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence drawer cannot open in the ruler-free list view

handleSilence in AlertRuleMenu sets showSilenceDrawer=true, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true and it requires `rulerRule={rule}`. In the list view RuleActionsButtons is now called with only promRule (see GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx line 47), so rule is undefined, the condition is false, and clicking 'Silence notifications' (which the new Grafana abilities can enable) does nothing.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete action is never rendered in the ruler-free list view

The Delete menu item is gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the new list view rulerRule is undefined by design (ruler requests were removed), so despite grafanaDeleteAbility being computed from promRule at lines 67-87, Delete never appears. This is confirmed by GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx, which grants AlertingRuleDelete and expects only 4 menu items with no Delete. Users cannot delete Grafana rules from the list view menu.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to block Update/Delete/Pause/Duplicate for federated (Mimir cross-tenant) groups. The refactor hard-codes `const isFederated = false` with only a TODO. CombinedRule consumers will now report federated rules as supported for edit/delete/pause (subject only to isEditable/isRemovable), allowing actions the backend/UI previously forbade for federated groups.

Grafana recording rules lose Pause/Restore abilities in list view

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates Pause and Restore (and ModifyExport/DeletePermanently) on `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, which is false for recording rules. The ruler-based implementation gated Pause on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which includes Grafana recording rules, and GrafanaPromRuleDTO carries isPaused for both types. In the ruler-free list view a recording rule can therefore no longer be paused/resumed (and AlertRuleMenu's pause item would be disabled even if it were rendered).

Pause action is never rendered in the ruler-free list view

The menu only renders MenuItemPauseRule when `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` is true. In the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem/GrafanaGroupLoader/FilterView) no rulerRule is passed, so rulerRule is undefined and the condition is always false, even though the PR computes grafanaPauseAbility from promRule at lines 67-83. Users in the alert list can therefore never pause/unpause a Grafana rule from this menu.

Rule link loses the returnTo parameter

The deleted GrafanaRuleLoader.GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` using createReturnTo(), so navigating back from the rule detail returned to the list with its filters. The new component builds the href with no query params, so the detail view loses the return-to-list context the old list item preserved.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting defeats the $__range guard

Queries are now passed through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on line 299 before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting() on line 300. querySupportsSplitting() (lines 282-289) relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) still seeing the literal $__range / $__range_s / $__range_ms variable, with the comment explaining such queries must not be split because the variable must be evaluated against the full, unsplit range. Once applyTemplateVariables expands that variable using the original request's range/scopedVars, the check can no longer detect it, so a query such as count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) is treated as splittable and is executed once per daily chunk, each chunk incorrectly using the full-range duration instead of being sent as a single unsplit request. This silently changes query semantics and results for $__range queries.

Shard-split queries are interpolated twice, including ad-hoc filter application

runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) on line 52, but the resulting targets are later passed to runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), which after this PR interpolates every target again with the same scopedVars and filters (querySplitting.ts line 299). Template interpolation is not guaranteed idempotent: applyTemplateVariables also applies ad-hoc filters to the expression, so shard-split queries with ad-hoc filters get the same label matcher/filter appended twice, and variable values introduced by the first expansion that contain $-patterns can be expanded again on the second pass. The updated test even codifies this by expecting applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for one original target. Shard splitting should either skip the second interpolation or not pass filters/re-interpolate already-interpolated targets, otherwise shard queries can produce duplicated or corrupted LogQL compared with the non-shard path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Plugin Request Completed" logs lose the explicit traceID field

logRequest previously added traceID (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log parameters, but that logic was removed and the replacement contextual attributes in ContextualLoggerMiddleware (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) do not include a trace ID. Unless infra/log.FromContext independently injects a trace ID, the completed-request log can no longer be correlated with traces by the traceID field that was present before this rename. The trace ID should be added to the contextual attributes or retained explicitly in logRequest.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the logger used to record log calls

FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing the receiver's recorded state). LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that constructs LoggerMiddleware with a TestLogger and asserts on that instance's InfoLogs will see zero calls because the message is recorded on a new, inaccessible TestLogger. The fake should return the receiver (f) so tests can observe logs emitted through FromContext.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to Logger breaks existing implementations of the interface

Logger is an interface, and this PR adds a required FromContext method to it. Only grafanaInfraLogWrapper and TestLogger in this repo's changed files are updated; any other implementations (other packages, generated/manual fakes, or downstream/enterprise code implementing plugins/log.Logger) will fail to compile until they add the method. This is a breaking interface change that should be called out and all in-tree implementations/fakes verified, or the method should be exposed via a separate optional interface.

Renamed middleware test keeps old name and provides no coverage for moved contextual logging

The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after the rename to MetricsMiddleware, and the PR adds a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware plus LoggerMiddleware's dependency on Logger.FromContext with no tests verifying that QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics contexts carry endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname or that LoggerMiddleware emits those fields. Rename the test and add coverage for the new middleware and its interaction with LoggerMiddleware so the moved contextual-logger behavior cannot silently regress.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded concurrently

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and then, in a separate DB session, inserts a new device if count < deviceLimit. There is no transaction, lock, or unique constraint enforcement tying the count to the insert, so many concurrent first-time requests from different devices can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. Under anonymous traffic (the exact load this feature limits) the cap is therefore not reliably enforced; enforcement needs to be serialized/atomic in the store.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Tagging moved from async background work to the synchronous auth path

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute background-context timeout and panic recovery; now Authenticate blocks on TagDevice (a CountDevices query plus an insert/update on cache miss) using the request context. This adds database latency to anonymous authentication, makes auth fail/slow when the store is slow, ties DB writes to request-context cancellation, and removes the panic recovery around tagging. Combined with the per-instance 29-minute cache, cache misses across many instances will also amplify DB load. If synchronous enforcement is required, it needs a bounded timeout/context handling rather than the raw request context.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing device inactive for >30 days is treated as over-limit instead of an existing device

When count >= deviceLimit, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within the last 30 days (anonymousDeviceExpiration). Devices are only deleted after 61 days (keepFor in impl.go), so a known device returning after 30-61 days still exists in anon_device but its UPDATE matches 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, denying a previously registered device. The stated intent ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') is not met for this window; existence should be checked separately from the 30-day activity window.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected device is cached as tagged, so a retry bypasses the limit

tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) before anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice/Authenticate deny that first request, but the device ID remains cached for the cache's 29-minute default lifetime. The next request hits the cache at line 83 and returns nil without touching the store, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds even though the device was never recorded and the limit is still reached. The limit therefore only denies the first attempt per device per instance; clients just retry to get in. The cache must only be populated after a successful store, and must be evicted on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider signature changed without regenerating Wire injection

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument, but no pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go changes are included. Grafana builds from the checked-in generated wire_gen.go, which still constructs AnonDBStore with one argument and passes it to ProvideAnonymousDeviceService where a db.DB is now expected, so the server package will not compile / DI is stale until `make wire` (or equivalent) is run and the generated file committed.

anonymousDeviceLimit contract mismatch: Go always sends 0, frontend type expects undefined for unset

AnonymousDeviceLimit is a plain int64 without omitempty, so an unconfigured instance (limit 0 = unlimited in the backend) serializes as anonymousDeviceLimit: 0. The frontend declares it `number | undefined` and GrafanaBootConfig defaults it to undefined to mean unset. Consumers cannot distinguish 'unlimited/0' from an explicitly configured value via the declared type, and any frontend logic checking for undefined to mean 'no limit' will never see it from a real server. Use a pointer/omitempty or document 0 as the unlimited sentinel consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch at Error level (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including on success paths where err is nil, and they include the complete ids slice and SQL condition. With the configured batch size this can dump tens of thousands of IDs into error logs once per batch until cleanup finishes, creating false error alerts/on-call noise, high log volume and serialization cost, and obscuring real failures. These progress messages should be Debug (or Info without the ID list), with Error reserved for the returned error path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs

The ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but this ticker drives CleanUpService.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history), not just annotation cleanup. Nothing in the PR description justifies a 10x increase in frequency for all of these jobs. This will increase database and filesystem load on every Grafana instance and shorten the effective timeout/interference window between full cleanup passes; it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or scoped/justified separately.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite and keys off configured batch size

deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when the database is SQLite and cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; otherwise it emits one '?' placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL also have bind-parameter limits (65535), so a user who raises annotation_cleanupjob_batchsize above that (the new test itself encourages very large batches such as 32767) will now get 'too many parameters' failures from the DELETE and cleanup will error on every cycle, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no host-parameter limit. The guard should be based on len(ids) and the actual dialect's parameter limit, chunking or inlining as needed per database.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) for elapsed storage time; Update does the same on storage failure (line 129). Delete records a successful storage duration using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label (line 106), creating wrong/high-cardinality series. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration (line 166). Dashboards/alerts based on these metrics will attribute failures and latency to the wrong backend and cannot be used to verify mode 3 legacy health.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled on return

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch legacy writes in goroutines using context.WithTimeoutCause derived from the incoming request ctx. That parent context is owned by the API-server request and may be cancelled as soon as the handler returns the unified-storage result, racing with or cancelling the legacy write. The 10s timeout does not detach the goroutine from the parent. Consequently the supposedly protective legacy copy can silently never be written, especially for slower legacy stores. The legacy context should be detached (for example context.WithoutCancel/background-derived) while preserving values, with only the new timeout applied.

Asynchronous legacy failures are not logged

The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only feed a duration metric and discard the error otherwise. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy failures with object context. If the legacy safety copy fails in mode 3, operators have no log message identifying the kind/name/error to reconcile the divergence; only an aggregate metric counter changes. Each goroutine should log the returned error (without relying on the possibly-cancelled request logger).

Legacy goroutines race with the caller on the shared object

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the asynchronous Legacy.Create, while immediately returning `created` to the caller. The caller/serializer and the legacy store can therefore read or mutate the same underlying object concurrently (for example resource version, UID or timestamps set by a store). Update similarly shares `objInfo` with an asynchronous legacy call after the synchronous storage update has already consumed it. This is a data race and can produce corrupted or inconsistent legacy writes; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy/computed object.

Mode 3 integration test synchronously asserts legacy visibility after async writes

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes through the k8s API and immediately checks the legacy playlist API (for example the legacy list/get checks inside doPlaylistTests). Because mode 3 now performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines, there is no happens-before guarantee that the legacy row exists when those assertions run. This makes the new file/unified-storage mode 3 integration cases flaky and can also hide eventual-consistency behaviour that needs polling with a timeout instead of immediate equality assertions.

Mode 3 tests never wait for or verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example Create at lines 30-32 and Update at lines 313-315) but return/assert immediately after the dual-writer call and never synchronize with the goroutine or call AssertCalled/AssertExpectations for the legacy mock. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is removed, cancelled, or never executes, and leaked goroutines can instead race with later tests using the shared mock/example objects. Tests need a synchronization/wait mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was invoked (and that failures are handled).

Mode 3 update no longer passes the storage-computed object to legacy

Update now passes the original `objInfo` directly to Legacy.Update. A registry Update implementation recomputes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the old object it loads from legacy storage, so legacy recomputes the update against a different (possibly missing or stale) old object instead of applying the exact object already committed to unified storage, as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did. This can make the asynchronous legacy update fail (for example NotFound/conflict) or diverge from unified storage while the API call reports success. The computed/returned storage object should be wrapped and passed to legacy.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

After the initial RLock check misses, every concurrent caller waits for the write lock and then unconditionally reloads assets-manifest.json and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache, even if another goroutine populated the cache while it was waiting. Because the file I/O is also performed while holding the exclusive lock, a cold-cache burst in non-Dev mode serializes redundant disk reads and blocks fast-path readers instead of only the first caller loading and the rest reusing the newly cached value. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring Lock (when cfg.Env != Dev) and return it if non-nil.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix

This change adds synchronization around the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, so the original race would not be reproduced or guarded against in CI (including with the race detector). A test should exercise parallel GetWebAssets calls on a cold cache (and, if feasible, in Dev mode where the cache is rewritten) against a temporary assets-manifest.json so a missing or incorrectly scoped lock fails under -race.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false through inverted dead logic

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), returns false when that value is true, and also returns false when it is false. The feature flag therefore has no effect and the branching is misleading: a maintainer trying to re-enable SQL expressions by restoring the flag check can easily invert the logic and either keep the feature permanently disabled or accidentally enable the unsafe DuckDB path. The helper should directly express the intended temporary disable (return false with a clear comment) or correctly return the flag value once the stub is removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No tests cover SQL-expression rejection and existing SQL tests are not updated

The PR disables SQL expressions in ReadQuery and stubs pkg/expr/sql.DB so TablesList, RunCommands, and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', but it adds no test asserting that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, and it does not update or skip the pre-existing tests that exercise TablesList/SQLCommand execution against DuckDB. Those existing tests will now fail against the stub, while the security-critical rejection path itself remains unprotected against regression. Add a reader test for the disabled SQL type and skip/remove/update the DuckDB-dependent tests accordingly.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command entry point is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand still accepts SQL expressions and calls NewSQLCommand without any feature-flag or disabled-feature check. It is only blocked incidentally because sql.TablesList now calls the stub DB and errors, producing a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. This leaves two different disable behaviours for SQL expressions (explicit rejection in ExpressionQueryReader versus an incidental parsing failure here), and if the stub DB's RunCommands/TablesList is ever partially restored this legacy path would again create executable SQLCommands without passing through the reader's guard. The legacy unmarshalling path should reject QueryTypeSQL explicitly as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key now race and can corrupt or leak indexes

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while building, and it unconditionally inserts b.cache[key]=idx at the end without checking whether another goroutine already built the same NamespacedResource. searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex does GetIndex (nil while a build is in flight) then BuildIndex, and searchSupport.init builds many keys in parallel, so two callers for the same key can now run bleve.New/NewMemOnly concurrently: for file-backed indexes both use the same directory path (bleve.New fails or contends on an existing/open index), for memory indexes one index is silently overwritten and the other leaked (with duplicate IndexTenants increments), and writes/searches can be split across the two instances. Previously the whole-build lock serialized this. A per-key build lock/singleflight or an existing-entry check under cacheMu before returning is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu while builds now insert concurrently

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock. With the finer-grained locking in this PR, BuildIndex now inserts into b.cache (line 138) concurrently with any TotalDocs call outside the init path, which is a Go data race and can panic with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock (and note DocCount on an index being flushed concurrently may also need care).

false_positives.candidate:
Handlers no longer consult initErr, so requests are served after Stop marks the server stopped

Every handler previously called s.Init(ctx), which (via sync.Once) returned s.initErr on subsequent calls; Stop() overwrites s.initErr with 'service is stopping/stopped', so post-Stop requests were rejected. With all per-handler Init calls removed, Create/Read/List/Search/etc. proceed against the backend after Stop has cancelled s.ctx and stopped the lifecycle, producing confusing backend errors or partially working requests instead of a clear stopped error. Either keep an explicit stopped/initErr check in handlers or gate serving elsewhere.

NewResourceServer now blocks on full index building and discards the server on init failure without cleanup

NewResourceServer unconditionally calls s.Init(ctx) with the internal background context (no timeout), so constructing a ResourceServer now synchronously builds every search index (GetResourceStats plus a full ListIterator scan per namespace) before any caller can serve or health-check it; construction that was previously cheap/lazy and only failed on first use now fails or hangs process startup, including for embedders that create the server but never serve unified-storage traffic. On init error it returns nil without calling s.cancel() or lifecycle Stop, even though search.init may already have started its background WatchWriteEvents goroutine (search.go uses context.Background()), leaking that goroutine and its backend poller.

init errgroup goroutines race on totalBatchesIndexed and the shared err variable

Inside group.Go, totalBatchesIndexed++ (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190) mutate variables captured from the enclosing scope without synchronization. Multiple workers run concurrently (and this PR makes their index builds actually parallel), so increments are lost and, more importantly, one goroutine's failure can be overwritten by another's nil error (or vice versa) before `return err` is read, causing init to report success despite a failed namespace build or a spurious failure. Use a local err per goroutine returned to errgroup and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes a literal "alias" provider instead of the created providers

Both cleanup registrations in testCacheIDPForLogin use testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") rather than the alias of the provider just created ("idp-alias-" + i, and similarly at line 425). The cleanup therefore targets a non-existent provider and the 20+ identity providers created by the test are left behind in the shared test realm, making the test suite order-dependent and potentially polluting other cache/count assertions; the cleanup should capture the per-iteration alias.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached getForLogin loses the delegate's result ordering

On a cache hit the method collects the cached internal IDs into a HashSet and returns identityProviders.stream(), so the order of the returned stream is hash iteration order of UUID strings instead of the order produced by the JPA delegate (which getAllStream returns in its deterministic query order). Any caller of getForLogin that does not explicitly re-sort (the login bean does, but the storage provider contract gives no sorting guarantee to other callers) will now see identity providers in a different, unstable order than before this caching was added.

getForLogin cache ignores organization-level invalidations

The login cache is keyed only by realm and FetchMode and getForLogin only checks isInvalid(cacheKey). Unlike getByOrganization (which also checks isInvalid(orgId)), it never checks whether the requested organizationId has been invalidated. Organization-side changes that register an invalidation for the organization id (organization update/removal and broker association changes performed through the organization provider rather than through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.create/update/remove) therefore do not evict the cached realm+mode IdentityProviderListQuery. The cached ID set keeps being served until an unrelated IdP mutation invalidates the login key, so brokers can remain visible for an organization they no longer belong to, or remain missing after being linked, on login pages.

getLoginPredicate can NPE on identity providers with a null config map

The new predicate unconditionally calls idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) for every org-linked identity provider. IdentityProviderModel allows the config to be set to null (e.g. models built/imported from representations without config), so evaluating this predicate during the new create/update/remove invalidation in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider will throw NullPointerException and fail the whole IdP operation, whereas the previous predicate only inspected enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin. The config access needs a null guard (treat missing config as not public).

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JCA provider

The method contract is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SunJSSE/SUN for PKCS12). Callers that use the returned provider by name/capability for signatures, key factories or certificate handling will silently get a non-BC provider with different algorithms and behaviour, instead of an honest null (as WildFlyElytronProvider returns) or an unsupported-operation signal.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks all external CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added as an abstract interface method rather than a default method. Any CryptoProvider implementation outside the four updated in-tree classes will fail to compile against this version, and already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order. A default order (e.g. 100) would let existing implementations keep working.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA test uses one P-256 key pair for ES384/ES512 and never verifies a signature

The constructor generates a single default (P-256) EC key pair, yet testES384 and testES512 pass it with signature lengths of 96 and 132 bytes, so the conversions are exercised on zero-padded/truncated values rather than real P-384/P-521 signatures. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to the same bytes; swapped or otherwise invalid R/S encodings would also pass. The test should generate a key pair per named curve and verify the DER-encoded result with Signature.verify against the public key.

Equal order() values make provider selection classpath-order dependent

DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() 200. When any two of them are present, the reversed sort leaves their relative order to ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order, which is not a defined contract, and the previous explicit 'multiple providers' failure is gone. The JVM can therefore silently start with e.g. the Elytron provider (whose getBouncyCastleProvider() returns null) instead of the default/FIPS provider depending on jar ordering.

Ignored crypto providers are still instantiated and mutate global security state

detectProvider streams the whole ServiceLoader before sorting, so every CryptoProvider on the classpath is constructed, not just the winner. DefaultCryptoProvider registers BouncyCastle with Security.addProvider and FIPS1402Provider inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at positions 1-3 and modifies security properties. Previously the multiple-provider case threw and aborted startup; now execution continues with the losing providers' global side effects still installed, which can pollute a FIPS deployment with a non-FIPS provider (or vice versa) while CryptoIntegration reports only the selected provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the all-Clients placeholder instead of client ids

getClientsWithPermission iterates every resource of type Clients and adds resource.getName() for granted resources. That iteration includes the all-resource resource whose name is literally 'Clients', while client-specific resources are named by client id. If the caller only has an all-Clients grant, the method returns {"Clients"} and none of the real client ids, so any consumer filtering clients by this id set will not match the clients the admin is permitted to access. Conversely it can expose a bogus identifier that is not a client. The all-resource case must be expanded to actual client ids (or excluded with callers handling the all-clients grant separately).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NullPointerException when the all-Clients resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no client-specific resource exists, the code loads the all-Clients resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the Clients resource is absent (e.g. the resource server was initialized before Clients support or the resource was not created), so the permission check throws NullPointerException instead of returning false. The String-scope overload in the same class does guard the analogous lookup, showing the missing check is an oversight; the result can be a 500 error on ordinary client view/manage/configure checks.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Clients scopes/resource

init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that already enabled FGAPv2 therefore keep a resource server created with only the Users scopes and the Users all-resource resource; the new Clients resource type, its 'Clients' all-resource resource, and the new scopes 'configure', 'map-roles-client-scope' and 'map-roles-composite' are never added. Creating Clients permissions in such realms will fail (missing scopes/resources) and client permission evaluation can hit missing-resource paths, so an upgrade/migration path for existing admin-permissions clients is required.

Resource display names are not resolved for the Clients resource type

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' for the all-resource resource and resolves a user id to a username for user-specific resources. The new Clients branch is missing, so Clients permissions fall through to resource.getDisplayName(). For the all-Clients resource that yields no meaningful 'All clients' label, and for client-specific resources whose name is the client UUID it yields the UUID/display name rather than the client's clientId. Authorization representations for Clients permissions will therefore show confusing or empty resource names in clients that consume getResourceName.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy deployments do not enable rolling-updates in the CR

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, before setting FeatureSpec.enabledFeatures to rolling-updates, so both parameterized tests run their default-strategy cases without the feature enabled in the Keycloak CR. The operator guide added in this PR states the rolling-updates feature must be enabled for operator update handling and shows it alongside the update strategy, so the default path's CR-level feature propagation is left untested; these cases can only pass because the shared custom test image bakes --features=rolling-updates in at build time (operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image), masking a regression for images that rely on the CR to enable the feature.

Feature-disabled exit-code contract is only partially tested

The new testFeatureNotEnabled test covers only the metadata subcommand and asserts only the stderr text. It does not cover the check subcommand, which has its own new Profile.isFeatureEnabled branch in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run(), and it does not assert exit code 4 (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) for either subcommand. The exit code is the documented scripting contract for this feature, so a regression that prints the message but exits 0, 1, or the old recreate code would pass this test while breaking automation that distinguishes feature-disabled (4) from recreate (3).

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW permission incorrectly grants global group manage permission

canManage() evaluates hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) against the all-groups resource, so an administrator granted only the view scope for all groups passes requireManage() checks such as creating a top-level group in GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup. Group creation/modification must require MANAGE only; VIEW should grant read access. This is a privilege-escalation bug not covered by the tests, which only verify creation with MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns and evaluates authorization-resource IDs instead of group IDs

For V2 group resources the group ID is stored as the resource name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and getOrCreateResource creates the resource with that as its name), while Resource.getId() is the authorization store's own resource UUID. This code passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission(String groupId, ...), which looks up resources by name, so specific-group resources are never found and evaluation falls back to the all-groups resource. It also adds groupResource.getId() to the returned set, but callers in UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource and getUsersCount expect actual group IDs for filtering users by group membership. The result is wrong user visibility/counts for admins with view-members/manage-members on specific groups.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing FGAP V2 realms never get the new Groups scopes/resource

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null, and this is the only place shown that creates the schema's scopes and all-resource-type resources. Realms that already enabled admin permissions before this change therefore keep a resource server with only the old Users/Clients scopes and resources: the Groups all-resource and the manage-membership/manage-members/view-members scopes are never added. Creating Groups scope permissions in such realms then fails scope resolution/validation, and group evaluations hit the missing-resource path, so the feature only works for newly initialized realms unless a migration/backfill is added.

hasPermission can throw NullPointerException when the all-groups resource does not exist

When no specific group resource is found, the code loads the all-groups resource via getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later constructs a ResourcePermission with it, without a null check. If the Groups type resource is absent (for example the resource server was initialized before it was created, or admin permissions resources were not (re)initialized), every canView/canManage/canViewMembers check for a group without its own resource throws an NPE instead of denying access.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian totpStep1 replaced with Italian text

totpStep1 in the Lithuanian (messages_lt) account bundle was changed to 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see instructions in the wrong language. Replace it with a Lithuanian translation of 'Install one of the following applications on your mobile:'.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.

The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Java MessageFormat syntax used in an i18next resource bundle

This account-ui bundle uses i18next interpolation everywhere else (e.g. {{0}}, {{name}}, <0>{{username}}</0>). Changing error-invalid-multivalued-size to Java MessageFormat syntax '{0} ... {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}' means the React/i18next renderer will not substitute the arguments or evaluate the choice; users will see the raw placeholders/choice expression instead of 'Attribute X must have at least ... and at most ... values'. The Java-style choice form belongs only in the server-side themes bundles, not this JS bundle.

Java MessageFormat syntax used in an i18next resource bundle

This admin-ui bundle is rendered by the JavaScript UI with i18next interpolation ({{0}} style). Changing error-invalid-multivalued-size to '{0} ... {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}' introduces Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat syntax that i18next cannot evaluate, so the validation message will be shown literally with unsubstituted placeholders instead of the attribute name and limits. Keep the {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} form for the JS bundle and use the choice form only in server-side message bundles.

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 replaced with Italian text

loginTotpStep1 in the Lithuanian (messages_lt) login bundle was changed to 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian, not Lithuanian. This is the same wrong-language copy-paste as in the account bundle and will show Italian instructions to Lithuanian users during TOTP setup. Use a Lithuanian translation instead.

Missing English bundle aborts verification with an unchecked exception

verifySafeHtml() derives the English file by regex-rewriting the input path and throws a raw RuntimeException when that file cannot be opened. This bypasses verify()'s contract of returning collected messages / throwing MojoExecutionException: a single locale file whose path does not rewrite to an existing _en.properties (e.g. a new locale, a locale containing characters outside [a-zA-Z-_], or a file verified standalone) crashes the whole plugin run instead of reporting a verification problem for that file. Catch this case and report it through the messages list or a MojoExecutionException naming both files.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId

Line 73 repeats Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") instead of checking rawTokenId. A null rawTokenId is therefore accepted and encodeTokenId() silently produces an id ending in ':null' (which then decodes to the literal string "null"), corrupting the token id instead of failing fast at construction.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted and off-by-one grant check

The encoded prefix is session(0-1)+tokenType(2-3)+grant(4-5), but the matcher checks substring(3,5) and returns false when that substring equals the expected grant shortcut. As written it rejects (partly) matching ids and accepts ids whose grant does not match, so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken no longer verify the grant type encoded in TOKEN_ID.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom grant factories

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an extension interface, but getShortcut() is added as an abstract method with no default implementation. Every existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory will fail to compile, and already-deployed implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all factories and calls getShortcut(). Token issuance/server startup can therefore break on upgrade; the method should have a default (e.g. unknown/na) implementation.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context was removed

The previously public Context(Context) copy constructor is deleted in this change. Code (including custom grant types/token-exchange code) that copied a grant Context will fail to compile and deployed binaries will fail with NoSuchMethodError. No replacement/deprecation is provided, so this is an unnecessary breaking API change in server-spi-private.

Token issuance now fails for any grant type without a registered shortcut

encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException when factory.getShortcutByGrantType() returns null, and TokenManager.initToken() now calls this for every access token. Previously a token could be issued for a grant/context whose grant_type string is not a registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory id (custom grants that call TokenManager directly, internal flows that set Constants.GRANT_TYPE themselves, or a grant factory returning no shortcut); now createClientAccessToken() aborts and no token is returned. Encoding context should fall back to the existing UNKNOWN ('na') shortcut instead of failing token issuance.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials can NPE and returns a credential without the stored id or label

getCredentials() dereferences getMyUser(user) without the null check used by isConfiguredFor(), so it can throw NullPointerException for a user absent from the map. When a user is present, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...) builds a fresh model from the raw codes, created date and (always unset) user label, discarding recoveryCodesModel.getId() and getUserLabel(); callers that rely on a stable credential id (display, deletion, removal when exhausted) therefore receive a null/ephemeral id and lose the label.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Exhausted federated recovery credential is not removed

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential now prefers a federated credential, but when allCodesUsed() is true this code calls removeStoredCredentialById(), which removes a locally stored credential and does not delete a credential held by user storage. The exhausted federated credential therefore remains configured for the user; although a required action is added, if that action is not completed the dead credential remains and subsequent recovery-code login can again select it instead of a valid local credential.

Federated recovery codes are sent and may be stored in plaintext, losing hashed model data

The local path stores RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, whose codes are hashed, together with its user label and generation time. The federated path instead serializes the raw generatedCodes list into UserCredentialModel. A user-storage provider that stores the challenge response as received therefore persists usable recovery codes in plaintext, so compromise of the external store exposes all unused codes. The label and generated-at values contained in credentialModel are also not transmitted. Send the hashed credential data/model in a defined format, or explicitly require and demonstrate hashing by the storage provider, rather than handing over the raw code list.

Login bean crashes when the selected federated credential has no unused code

The bean now selects a federated credential first and unconditionally calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get(). If that federated credential is present but all its codes are used (which can happen because the authenticator cannot remove federated credentials via removeStoredCredentialById), getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() is empty and this throws NoSuchElementException, breaking rendering of the login form instead of treating the user as having no usable recovery credential or forcing regeneration.

Test user-storage validator does not consume used recovery codes

isValid() returns true whenever the submitted code matches any code in the stored JSON list, but it never removes or marks that code as used. Consequently the same recovery code can be replayed for unlimited logins for federated users in this provider, unlike local recovery codes which are single-use. The new test logs in only once, so this replay behaviour is not detected; update the stored credential to consume the matched code (and add a reuse-fails test).

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, making the new concurrency test racy and leaky

The test starts a reader thread looping while deletedAll is false, then sets deletedAll=true at line 155 and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty at line 157 without joining the thread. An iteration already inside groups() can still add an exception after the assertion (false pass), or the still-running thread can leak into subsequent tests using the same managed realm/admin client and add failures there. The tight loop also hammers the server with no pause, so unrelated client/timeout errors can be collected unboundedly in the CopyOnWriteArrayList and make the test flaky. The thread should be stored, joined (with timeout) before asserting, and terminated in a finally block.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent-deletion NPE remains in other lazy-delegate accessors

The fix null-checks modelSupplier.get() only in getSubGroupsCount(), but the same lazy delegate is dereferenced without a null check in getSubGroupsStream(String,Integer,Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer,Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String,Boolean,Integer,Integer) at line 268. When another transaction deletes the group, LazyModel/getGroupById returns null exactly as in the getSubGroupsCount() case, so these methods still throw NullPointerException instead of handling the deleted group. The reported concurrent-access NPE therefore remains reachable through subgroup listing/search paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() stops terminating remaining flusher processes after the deadline expires

join() sets the shared stopped flag and then iterates over all flusher processes, but if waiting for an early process consumes the deadline, the `break` at lines 339-341 exits the loop before terminate() is attempted for every later process. Those daemon flusher processes can therefore keep polling Redis and producing segments after the strategy has supposedly joined, including after a rebalance or shutdown, and can compete with a replacement flusher for the same shards. All processes should be terminated even when the waiting deadline has already expired.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the loop when the deadline expires skips calling terminate() on the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid flusher process counts are not rejected and can disable flushing

The CLI accepts any integer for --flusher-processes and SpanFlusher performs no validation. A negative value makes num_processes negative at line 60, producing an empty process_to_shards_map and spawning no flusher at all, while submit() finds no backpressure values and continues accepting spans into Redis indefinitely. A value of 0 passed programmatically is also silently changed by `max_processes or len(...)` into one process per shard instead of being rejected or honored. The process count should be validated as >= 1 at the CLI/factory/flusher boundary.

Restarting a hung threaded flusher creates a duplicate flusher for the same shards

When produce_to_pipe is used, flushers are threading.Thread objects. _ensure_processes_alive() detects a hang, but the kill at lines 253-257 is skipped because a thread is not a multiprocessing.Process, and _create_process_for_shards() then starts a second thread for the same shards while the hung thread may later resume. Both threads can call flush_segments(), produce the same segment, and call done_flush_segments() for the same shards, risking duplicate buffered segments. Overwriting self.processes[process_index] also loses the only handle to the old thread, so join() can no longer wait for or stop it.

Multi-process flusher test never verifies that shared-process shards actually flush

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the number of processes and that four shard ids appear in process_to_shards_map; it submits no spans and asserts no produced segment for any shard. A regression in the shard-subset SpansBuffer construction, the new SpanFlusher.main() argument order, or flushing when multiple shards share one process/thread would therefore still pass. The test should push spans for shards handled by both processes and assert the flushed output.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
