false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore commit past a message whose processing failed, so it will never be retried or sent to a DLQ. This directly contradicts the strategy docstring claiming it only commits offsets after successful processing and can silently lose uptime results.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected when workers fall behind. Arroyo will keep submitting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them, accumulating decoded WorkItems (including the original Kafka message) in memory indefinitely, growing OffsetTracker sets for uncommittable partitions as well. A slow subscription or downstream outage therefore risks OOM and massive reprocessing on restart rather than natural backpressure as claimed in the class docstring.

Shared queue pool is destroyed by the first strategy close and reused after rebalance

The FixedQueuePool (and its worker threads and OffsetTracker) is created once on the factory and handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo creates/closes strategies on partition assignment and rebalance; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down that shared pool, and queue.Queue.put() on a shut-down queue raises ShutDown. The next assignment reuses the same dead pool (factory only nulls it in factory.shutdown(), not on strategy close), so subsequent messages fail to enqueue, are swallowed by submit()'s broad except handler, and are marked complete without processing. The shared OffsetTracker also retains last_committed across assignments, so a partition reassigned at a lower offset can never be committed again.

Close stops committing before queued work is drained

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, and it never waits for queues to empty. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so a worker that finishes its current item exits at the loop condition instead of draining remaining queued items. Consequently queued items are abandoned on graceful shutdown and any items workers do finish after the commit thread stops never have their offsets committed, causing avoidable duplicate reprocessing and violating the graceful-shutdown expectation.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() on a string group key. For strings, hash() is randomized per interpreter process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the same subscription maps to different queues in different processes and across restarts. That breaks the documented consistent-assignment/ordering guarantee whenever work for a group moves between consumer processes or the consumer restarts, and makes distribution non-reproducible; a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5, as used elsewhere in the uptime consumer) should be used instead.

Submit swallows grouping/decoder failures and marks the offset complete

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one broad except that logs the error and then add_offset()+complete_offset()s the message. Any failure in grouping_fn (or an enqueue failure such as a shut-down queue) therefore makes the message eligible for offset commit even though it was never processed, silently dropping it instead of surfacing the failure to Arroyo for retry/DLQ handling.

false_positives.candidate:
ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM, corrupting scores of spans present in both sets

Both zunionstore calls omit AGGREGATE/WEIGHTS, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both the destination and source sorted sets. A span payload already in set_key that is also in span_key/parent_key (duplicate delivery or overlapping merge) gets its end_timestamp_precise roughly doubled, moving it to ~year 2077. That corrupts the ordering used by ZPOPMIN eviction: duplicated spans become effectively unevictable while legitimate spans are evicted instead. The old SUNIONSTORE had no such side effect; AGGREGATE MAX (or equivalent) is required.

Set-to-sorted-set conversion breaks on all pre-existing Redis buffer keys

process_spans now ZADDs into span-buf:s:* keys that existing deployments hold as Redis SETs (previously SADD), and the Lua script and _load_segment_data now use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN on them. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these commands on set-typed keys, so every in-flight segment buffered before deploy will fail processing/flushing until its TTL (up to redis_ttl, 3600s) expires, stalling or erroring batches. There is no key versioning, migration, or type check in the PR.

New required Span field inserted before a defaulted field breaks existing constructors

end_timestamp_precise is added as a required positional field immediately before is_segment_span, which previously was the seventh positional/keyword field with a default. Any Span(...) construction elsewhere (other consumers, scripts, tests not in this diff) that omits the new field now raises TypeError, and any construction passing is_segment_span positionally will silently assign a bool as end_timestamp_precise, which then becomes a Redis sorted-set score of 0/1. Adding it at the end with a default, or updating all call sites verifiably, is needed.

Direct indexing of end_timestamp_precise turns a missing field into a poison-pill batch

process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] for every Kafka message. Previously this field was not read, and the updated tests themselves show messages legitimately lacking it before this change. A single span without the field raises KeyError, failing the whole batch; with Arroyo retries this becomes a poison pill blocking the partition. A defensive .get with a fallback (e.g. end_timestamp or 0) or explicit schema guarantee plus dead-letter handling is needed.

Insert-time eviction silently discards the earliest-ending spans, possibly the segment span

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN silently deletes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise with no metric, log, or downstream signal. The flushed segment is then emitted as if complete while missing spans; if an evicted span carried parent/redirect relationships, or the segment span itself is evicted for long-running roots whose children end later, flush_segments marks no span is_segment and produces a rootless segment under the wrong segment_id. The hard-coded 1000 also disagrees with SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans=1001 and ignores the configurable limit entirely.

Flush-time max_segment_spans enforcement removed without an equivalent guarantee

_load_segment_data no longer aborts segments exceeding self.max_segment_spans; it now loads and returns arbitrarily many spans (bounded only by the 10MiB byte check). The Lua cap does not fully replace this: it is hard-coded to 1000 rather than the configured value, only runs on the insert/merge path for the final set_key, and does not protect against keys created or grown outside that path (including pre-existing keys). Oversized segments that were previously skipped with a metric/error will now be produced downstream.

Redirect chain limit cut from 10000 to 1000 regresses deep segment trees

The redirect-following loop limit drops from 10000 to 1000 iterations (and the explanatory comment is deleted). For span trees deeper than 1000 redirects — previously supported up to 10k — set_span_id stops mid-chain, so the span is written to a wrong/intermediate set and the segment is split into multiple segments that flush separately with incorrect segment_ids. This is an unannounced behavioral regression unrelated to the eviction change.

No test covers eviction, score merging, or the new paginator path

All updated buffer tests use identical end_timestamp_precise values and at most 5 spans, so the headline behavior — eviction above 1000 spans, which spans are chosen for eviction, ZUNIONSTORE score handling for duplicates, and ordering by end time — is entirely untested, as is OptimizedCursorPaginator/negative offsets and the audit-log optimized branch. The regressions above (score summing, root eviction, datetime paginator crash, negative-slice crash) would all pass the current suite.

_is_error_focused_query ignores the query argument passed through _get_event_stats and only inspects request.GET['query']. Callers that synthesize or modify the query (for example the dashboard split path builds '(query) AND !event.type:transaction' for the errors-only probe) therefore get eligibility decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, so genuinely error-only split queries are not upsampled unless the original GET parameter happens to contain 'event.type:error'. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility decision.

upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered on Discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform always returns True for the errors dataset, causing count() to be rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count', but the new SnQLFunction is only added to DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter in discover.py; the errors dataset config is untouched. A request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore send an unregistered function to the errors query builder and fail validation instead of returning stats. Register upsampled_count for the errors dataset (and any other dataset for which the transform is enabled) or restrict the transform to datasets that define it; the added Snuba tests never exercise dataset=errors.

sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight

The upsampled_count aggregate is a bare sum(sample_weight) wrapped in toInt64. Events in allowlisted projects that were ingested without error sampling (or before sample_weight was populated) have a NULL/0 sample_weight, so they contribute nothing and can make an entire bucket NULL/0 instead of counting once, silently under-reporting historical and unsampled errors. The aggregate should treat a missing weight as 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce/ifNull(sample_weight, 1))) so unsampled events count normally.

Stray nested-repository pointer file committed

This adds a top-level file named 'sentry-repo' whose entire content is 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental gitlink/submodule artifact without any .gitmodules entry. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, pollutes the repository root, and can confuse tooling that scans the tree. Remove the file before merging.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' without escaping or length-prefixing. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct triples produce the same key: for example name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both produce "..._dashboards:read_a_b_c". A denial for one resource can consequently fast-path-deny a different resource for 30 seconds. Use an unambiguous encoding such as separated, escaped, or hashed components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple underscore concatenation to build the cache key, leading to key collisions when components contain underscores, which causes incorrect permission denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache key omits identity type and can poison renderer checks

The denial key is built only from namespace, raw subject UID, action, name, and parent folder, ignoring checkReq.IdentityType. Anonymous subjects and the render service both commonly use UID "0"; an anonymous denial for dashboards:read on a dashboard is therefore cached under the same key as a render-service check for that dashboard. The later render check returns Allowed:false from permDenialCache before getRendererPermissions can return its wildcard read permission, incorrectly breaking rendering for up to the 30-second denial TTL. Include the identity type (or do not denial-cache synthetic identities such as renderer) in the key.

Denials caused by the stale folder tree are cached, extending folder staleness

On a cached-permission miss Check re-queries permissions from the DB, but checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions still resolve ancestors through buildFolderTree, which returns the short-TTL cached folder tree without refreshing it. For a dashboard whose access is inherited from an ancestor above its immediate parent, a newly created/re-parented folder can therefore still produce Allowed:false, and lines 153-155 then write that result into permDenialCache. The false denial is now pinned for another denial-cache TTL even after the folder tree refreshes, partially defeating the PR's goal for newly created folders. Do not denial-cache denials that depended on the folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the DB fallback path.

Every denied check for a new resource name bypasses the permission cache to the DB

If cached permissions do not allow the requested name, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which after this PR always queries the permission store. The denial cache only helps repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent); a caller probing or enumerating many distinct dashboard/folder names—each a distinct denial key—forces a full permission DB query per name, with singleflight only deduplicating concurrent identical requests. This removes the previous cache protection against sequential negative-check DB load and needs a bound (for example revalidate at most once per cached permission-set generation/TTL window) rather than per-resource requery.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

After the initial RLock check misses, every concurrent caller waits for the write lock and then unconditionally reloads assets-manifest.json and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache, even if another goroutine populated the cache while it was waiting. Because the file I/O is also performed while holding the exclusive lock, a cold-cache burst in non-Dev mode serializes redundant disk reads and blocks fast-path readers instead of only the first caller loading and the rest reusing the newly cached value. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) for elapsed storage time; Update does the same on storage failure (line 129). Delete records a successful storage duration using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label (line 106), creating wrong/high-cardinality series. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration (line 166). Dashboards/alerts based on these metrics will attribute failures and latency to the wrong backend and cannot be used to verify mode 3 legacy health.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact problem mentioned in the golden comment: 'Delete records a successful storage duration using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label (line 106)', alongside other related metrics recording issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled on return

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch legacy writes in goroutines using context.WithTimeoutCause derived from the incoming request ctx. That parent context is owned by the API-server request and may be cancelled as soon as the handler returns the unified-storage result, racing with or cancelling the legacy write. The 10s timeout does not detach the goroutine from the parent. Consequently the supposedly protective legacy copy can silently never be written, especially for slower legacy stores. The legacy context should be detached (for example context.WithoutCancel/background-derived) while preserving values, with only the new timeout applied.

Legacy goroutines race with the caller on the shared object

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the asynchronous Legacy.Create, while immediately returning `created` to the caller. The caller/serializer and the legacy store can therefore read or mutate the same underlying object concurrently (for example resource version, UID or timestamps set by a store). Update similarly shares `objInfo` with an asynchronous legacy call after the synchronous storage update has already consumed it. This is a data race and can produce corrupted or inconsistent legacy writes; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy/computed object.

Mode 3 update no longer passes the storage-computed object to legacy

Update now passes the original `objInfo` directly to Legacy.Update. A registry Update implementation recomputes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the old object it loads from legacy storage, so legacy recomputes the update against a different (possibly missing or stale) old object instead of applying the exact object already committed to unified storage, as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did. This can make the asynchronous legacy update fail (for example NotFound/conflict) or diverge from unified storage while the API call reports success. The computed/returned storage object should be wrapped and passed to legacy.

Asynchronous legacy failures are not logged

The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only feed a duration metric and discard the error otherwise. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy failures with object context. If the legacy safety copy fails in mode 3, operators have no log message identifying the kind/name/error to reconcile the divergence; only an aggregate metric counter changes. Each goroutine should log the returned error (without relying on the possibly-cancelled request logger).

Mode 3 tests never wait for or verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example Create at lines 30-32 and Update at lines 313-315) but return/assert immediately after the dual-writer call and never synchronize with the goroutine or call AssertCalled/AssertExpectations for the legacy mock. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is removed, cancelled, or never executes, and leaked goroutines can instead race with later tests using the shared mock/example objects. Tests need a synchronization/wait mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was invoked (and that failures are handled).

Mode 3 integration test synchronously asserts legacy visibility after async writes

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes through the k8s API and immediately checks the legacy playlist API (for example the legacy list/get checks inside doPlaylistTests). Because mode 3 now performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines, there is no happens-before guarantee that the legacy row exists when those assertions run. This makes the new file/unified-storage mode 3 integration cases flaky and can also hide eventual-consistency behaviour that needs polling with a timeout instead of immediate equality assertions.

Queries are now passed through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on line 299 before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting() on line 300. querySupportsSplitting() (lines 282-289) relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) still seeing the literal $__range / $__range_s / $__range_ms variable, with the comment explaining such queries must not be split because the variable must be evaluated against the full, unsplit range. The updated test even codifies this by expecting applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for one original target. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and then, in a separate DB session, inserts a new device if count < deviceLimit. true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Tagging moved from async background work to the synchronous auth path

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute background-context timeout and panic recovery; now Authenticate blocks on TagDevice (a CountDevices query plus an insert/update on cache miss) using the request context. This adds database latency to anonymous authentication, makes auth fail/slow when the store is slow, ties DB writes to request-context cancellation, and removes the panic recovery around tagging. Combined with the per-instance 29-minute cache, cache misses across many instances will also amplify DB load. If synchronous enforcement is required, it needs a bounded timeout/context handling rather than the raw request context.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same code change: moving `TagDevice` from an asynchronous background goroutine to the synchronous `Authenticate` path. While the golden comment specifically highlights that `ErrDeviceLimitReached` will now block authentication, and the candidate focuses more on DB latency, errors, and context cancellation blocking authentication, they both point to the same underlying architectural change and the resulting risk that `TagDevice` failures/delays now fail/block anonymous authentication.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing device inactive for >30 days is treated as over-limit instead of an existing device

When count >= deviceLimit, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within the last 30 days (anonymousDeviceExpiration). Devices are only deleted after 61 days (keepFor in impl.go), so a known device returning after 30-61 days still exists in anon_device but its UPDATE matches 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, denying a previously registered device. The stated intent ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') is not met for this window; existence should be checked separately from the 30-day activity window.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug in `updateDevice`: when an UPDATE matches 0 rows ( specifically because the device falls outside the 30-day time window), the function erroneously returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The candidate issue provides more context about the 30-61 day retention window, while the golden comment is more general about why 0 rows affected doesn't mean the limit was reached, though both point to the exact same flawed logic and error return.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected device is cached as tagged, so a retry bypasses the limit

tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) before anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice/Authenticate deny that first request, but the device ID remains cached for the cache's 29-minute default lifetime. The next request hits the cache at line 83 and returns nil without touching the store, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds even though the device was never recorded and the limit is still reached. The limit therefore only denies the first attempt per device per instance; clients just retry to get in. The cache must only be populated after a successful store, and must be evicted on error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue describe the exact same bug: `tagDeviceUI` sets the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` occurs, the device ID remains cached for 29 minutes, allowing subsequent requests to hit the cache and bypass the device limit.

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument, but no pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go changes are included. anonymousDeviceLimit contract mismatch: Go always sends 0, frontend type expects undefined for unset

AnonymousDeviceLimit is a plain int64 without omitempty, so an unconfigured instance (limit 0 = unlimited in the backend) serializes as anonymousDeviceLimit: 0. The frontend declares it `number | undefined` and GrafanaBootConfig defaults it to undefined to mean unset. Consumers cannot distinguish 'unlimited/0' from an explicitly configured value via the declared type, and any frontend logic checking for undefined to mean 'no limit' will never see it from a real server. Use a pointer/omitempty or document 0 as the unlimited sentinel consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback translations can be permanently cached as missing

I18n.translate only loads config.locale before consulting the LRU cache, not the fallback locales configured in config/initializers/i18n.rb. If a no-argument translation is first looked up when its fallback locale (site default or :en) has not been loaded, translate_no_cache returns a 'translation missing' string and lines 71-76 freeze and cache it under the current locale. Loading the fallback locale later does not invalidate @cache, so the missing-translation string keeps being served until LRU eviction or reload, defeating the fallback feature.

Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests

ensure_loaded! is only called from ApplicationController#set_locale. Server-side translations also happen in background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console and model code, where no controller before_filter runs. In those contexts I18n.translate loads only the current locale, so keys missing from that locale but present in the site-default or English files return 'translation missing' instead of falling back, making the feature inconsistent between requests and jobs/mailers.

FallbackLocaleList breaks the I18n.fallbacks Hash contract

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but overrides [] to ignore anything stored in the hash and always synthesize a value. Code using the documented I18n fallbacks API, e.g. I18n.fallbacks[:de] = [:fr] or the Fallbacks#map helper provided by the i18n gem/Rails, will write entries that are never read back, and enumeration/keys/empty? report an empty hash even though [] returns entries. Per-locale fallback customization is therefore silently discarded.

Every fallback lookup queries SiteSetting and crashes if it is unset

The i18n Fallbacks backend calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on each translation lookup, and this implementation calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym every time. That ties hot-path translation (including translations with arguments, which bypass the accelerator cache) to the DB-backed settings store, adds a settings lookup per translation, breaks translations performed before the database/settings are available (boot, migrations), and raises NoMethodError if default_locale is ever nil instead of degrading to :en.

No tests cover the new fallback ordering or loading behavior

The PR adds a custom FallbackLocaleList, a new I18n.ensure_loaded!, and a per-request loading hook, and removes the Rails config.i18n.fallbacks settings, but adds no specs. There is no coverage that a missing key in the user locale resolves to the site-default then English text, that duplicate locales (user == default == :en) are de-duplicated, or that fallback files are loaded in non-controller contexts, so the cache-poisoning and jobs/mailers gaps above can regress undetected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write save during validation, double-counting and losing concurrent updates

should_block? is called from EmailValidator during User validation, yet it mutates and saves the BlockedEmail record (`match_count += 1; last_match_at = ...; record.save`). Validation is not a single occurrence: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which re-validates, so one signup attempt increments match_count at least twice, and any other `valid?` check also permanently increments it even if the user is never saved. Multiple date overrides on the same day are handled incorrectly

With two override ranges on the same day, a slot inside the first range but outside the second makes find succeed and the function returns false, incorrectly hiding slots that are inside one of the day's overrides.

Override conversion assumes timeZone is present and loses day overflow

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` update instead.

Any existing consumer calling service.findMany(...) will now fail TypeScript compilation (and would fail at runtime if untyped), breaking the insights data path until every call site is migrated.

Event-type filter returns an unparenthesized OR expression

buildFilterConditions stores the event-type condition as `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` with no parentheses around the whole OR, and when it is the only filter getFilterConditions returns that fragment unchanged. getBaseConditions happens to wrap it, but the public getFilterConditions result is unsafe to interpolate into a larger WHERE clause: `WHERE "userId" = 1 OR "eventParentId" = 2 AND <other>` is parsed by PostgreSQL as `"userId" = 1 OR ("eventParentId" = 2 AND <other>)` because AND binds tighter than OR, so rows can be returned that ignore the additional constraints. The previous structured Prisma where-object preserved this grouping automatically. The fragment should be wrapped as `((...) OR (...))` at construction.

Multi-branch authorization conditions are not wrapped as a single expression

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition reduce their branches to `(<branch A>) OR (<branch B>)` without enclosing the complete OR in parentheses, and the single-branch case returns a bare AND expression. getBaseConditions wraps the result, but the public getAuthorizationConditions result loses the grouping guarantee the old Prisma where-object provided: a caller interpolating it as `WHERE ${auth} AND <date/status condition>` gets `branchA OR (branchB AND <condition>)`, so branch A rows bypass the caller's date/status restrictions. This PR removes the entire 'Caching' describe block that verified repeated getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions calls return cached results, but the service still implements that caching (cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions in insightsBooking.ts). The surrounding try/catch (lines 124-139) also cannot catch rejections from the async callback, so failures become unhandled rejections instead of being logged. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (or a for...of loop) so deletion completes and errors are handled.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, not lazily

Every value in the appStore object literal is an immediately invoked import() (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")` on line 3 and likewise for all ~29 apps). Evaluating this object when the module is first imported therefore starts loading every app at once, so importing appStore from any file (getCalendar, videoClient, payment handlers, routers) still pulls in all apps and defeats the lazy/on-demand loading this PR is meant to achieve. The values need to be thunks (e.g. `() => import(...)`) with call sites invoking them, or an equivalent lazy lookup, to actually defer loading until an app is requested.

appStore value type changed from module to Promise without a compatible accessor

appStore previously mapped each key to a module namespace object, so consumers could synchronously use `appStore[key].lib`, `'lib' in appStore[key]`, etc. It now maps each key to a Promise of the module, which is not backward compatible: any consumer not converted to `await appStore[key]` in this PR will receive a Promise, find no `lib` property (`'lib' in promise` is false), and silently skip calendar/video/payment functionality (or fail type-checking). This PR only updates a subset of call sites, so the exported contract break needs either a full audit/conversion of every appStore consumer or a compatibility-preserving accessor.

async forEach callback makes reschedule deletion fire-and-forget

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` discards each callback's promise. The mutation then immediately sends the reschedule email, fires webhooks, and returns, so the calendar/video deletions for the old booking may not have started, let alone finished; if the request context is torn down they are silently dropped and the old events remain. Rejections inside the callback are also unhandled. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` before sending email/webhooks.

Recurring-booking calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes after it is awaited

In the recurring-cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials...forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` runs its pushes only after awaiting getCalendar (now a dynamic import) and deleteEvent. Later, `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) snapshots whatever apiDeletes contains at that moment, so entries pushed afterwards are never awaited; the handler can delete booking references/attendees and report success while the recurring calendar events are never deleted. Convert this branch to a for...of loop or collect the per-credential work with Promise.all and push/await those promises, as was done for the non-recurring branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

join() sets the shared stopped flag and then iterates over all flusher processes, but if waiting for an early process consumes the deadline, the `break` at lines 339-341 exits the loop before terminate() is attempted for every later process. Those daemon flusher processes can therefore keep polling Redis and producing segments after the strategy has supposedly joined, including after a rebalance or shutdown, and can compete with a replacement flusher for the same shards. All processes should be terminated even when the waiting deadline has already expired.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that breaking out of the loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown, and recommend attempting termination regardless of the deadline.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid flusher process counts are not rejected and can disable flushing

The CLI accepts any integer for --flusher-processes and SpanFlusher performs no validation. A negative value makes num_processes negative at line 60, producing an empty process_to_shards_map and spawning no flusher at all, while submit() finds no backpressure values and continues accepting spans into Redis indefinitely. A value of 0 passed programmatically is also silently changed by `max_processes or len(...)` into one process per shard instead of being rejected or honored. The process count should be validated as >= 1 at the CLI/factory/flusher boundary.

Restarting a hung threaded flusher creates a duplicate flusher for the same shards

When produce_to_pipe is used, flushers are threading.Thread objects. _ensure_processes_alive() detects a hang, but the kill at lines 253-257 is skipped because a thread is not a multiprocessing.Process, and _create_process_for_shards() then starts a second thread for the same shards while the hung thread may later resume. Both threads can call flush_segments(), produce the same segment, and call done_flush_segments() for the same shards, risking duplicate buffered segments. Overwriting self.processes[process_index] also loses the only handle to the old thread, so join() can no longer wait for or stop it.

Multi-process flusher test never verifies that shared-process shards actually flush

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the number of processes and that four shard ids appear in process_to_shards_map; it submits no spans and asserts no produced segment for any shard. A regression in the shard-subset SpansBuffer construction, the new SpanFlusher.main() argument order, or flushing when multiple shards share one process/thread would therefore still pass. The test should push spans for shards handled by both processes and assert the flushed output.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

init errgroup goroutines race on totalBatchesIndexed and the shared err variable

Inside group.Go, totalBatchesIndexed++ (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190) mutate variables captured from the enclosing scope without synchronization. Multiple workers run concurrently (and this PR makes their index builds actually parallel), so increments are lost and, more importantly, one goroutine's failure can be overwritten by another's nil error (or vice versa) before `return err` is read, causing init to report success despite a failed namespace build or a spurious failure. Use a local err per goroutine returned to errgroup and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

NewResourceServer now blocks on full index building and discards the server on init failure without cleanup

NewResourceServer unconditionally calls s.Init(ctx) with the internal background context (no timeout), so constructing a ResourceServer now synchronously builds every search index (GetResourceStats plus a full ListIterator scan per namespace) before any caller can serve or health-check it; construction that was previously cheap/lazy and only failed on first use now fails or hangs process startup, including for embedders that create the server but never serve unified-storage traffic. On init error it returns nil without calling s.cancel() or lifecycle Stop, even though search.init may already have started its background WatchWriteEvents goroutine (search.go uses context.Background()), leaking that goroutine and its backend poller.

Handlers no longer consult initErr, so requests are served after Stop marks the server stopped

Every handler previously called s.Init(ctx), which (via sync.Once) returned s.initErr on subsequent calls; Stop() overwrites s.initErr with 'service is stopping/stopped', so post-Stop requests were rejected. With all per-handler Init calls removed, Create/Read/List/Search/etc. proceed against the backend after Stop has cancelled s.ctx and stopped the lifecycle, producing confusing backend errors or partially working requests instead of a clear stopped error. Either keep an explicit stopped/initErr check in handlers or gate serving elsewhere.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore commit past a message whose processing failed, so it will never be retried or sent to a DLQ. This directly contradicts the strategy docstring claiming it only commits offsets after successful processing and can silently lose uptime results.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected when workers fall behind. Arroyo will keep submitting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them, accumulating decoded WorkItems (including the original Kafka message) in memory indefinitely, growing OffsetTracker sets for uncommittable partitions as well. A slow subscription or downstream outage therefore risks OOM and massive reprocessing on restart rather than natural backpressure as claimed in the class docstring.

Shared queue pool is destroyed by the first strategy close and reused after rebalance

The FixedQueuePool (and its worker threads and OffsetTracker) is created once on the factory and handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo creates/closes strategies on partition assignment and rebalance; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down that shared pool, and queue.Queue.put() on a shut-down queue raises ShutDown. The next assignment reuses the same dead pool (factory only nulls it in factory.shutdown(), not on strategy close), so subsequent messages fail to enqueue, are swallowed by submit()'s broad except handler, and are marked complete without processing. The shared OffsetTracker also retains last_committed across assignments, so a partition reassigned at a lower offset can never be committed again.

Close stops committing before queued work is drained

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, and it never waits for queues to empty. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so a worker that finishes its current item exits at the loop condition instead of draining remaining queued items. Consequently queued items are abandoned on graceful shutdown and any items workers do finish after the commit thread stops never have their offsets committed, causing avoidable duplicate reprocessing and violating the graceful-shutdown expectation.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() on a string group key. For strings, hash() is randomized per interpreter process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the same subscription maps to different queues in different processes and across restarts. That breaks the documented consistent-assignment/ordering guarantee whenever work for a group moves between consumer processes or the consumer restarts, and makes distribution non-reproducible; a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5, as used elsewhere in the uptime consumer) should be used instead.

Submit swallows grouping/decoder failures and marks the offset complete

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one broad except that logs the error and then add_offset()+complete_offset()s the message. Any failure in grouping_fn (or an enqueue failure such as a shut-down queue) therefore makes the message eligible for offset commit even though it was never processed, silently dropping it instead of surfacing the failure to Arroyo for retry/DLQ handling.

false_positives.candidate:
ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM, corrupting scores of spans present in both sets

Both zunionstore calls omit AGGREGATE/WEIGHTS, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both the destination and source sorted sets. A span payload already in set_key that is also in span_key/parent_key (duplicate delivery or overlapping merge) gets its end_timestamp_precise roughly doubled, moving it to ~year 2077. That corrupts the ordering used by ZPOPMIN eviction: duplicated spans become effectively unevictable while legitimate spans are evicted instead. The old SUNIONSTORE had no such side effect; AGGREGATE MAX (or equivalent) is required.

Set-to-sorted-set conversion breaks on all pre-existing Redis buffer keys

process_spans now ZADDs into span-buf:s:* keys that existing deployments hold as Redis SETs (previously SADD), and the Lua script and _load_segment_data now use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN on them. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these commands on set-typed keys, so every in-flight segment buffered before deploy will fail processing/flushing until its TTL (up to redis_ttl, 3600s) expires, stalling or erroring batches. There is no key versioning, migration, or type check in the PR.

New required Span field inserted before a defaulted field breaks existing constructors

end_timestamp_precise is added as a required positional field immediately before is_segment_span, which previously was the seventh positional/keyword field with a default. Any Span(...) construction elsewhere (other consumers, scripts, tests not in this diff) that omits the new field now raises TypeError, and any construction passing is_segment_span positionally will silently assign a bool as end_timestamp_precise, which then becomes a Redis sorted-set score of 0/1. Adding it at the end with a default, or updating all call sites verifiably, is needed.

Direct indexing of end_timestamp_precise turns a missing field into a poison-pill batch

process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] for every Kafka message. Previously this field was not read, and the updated tests themselves show messages legitimately lacking it before this change. A single span without the field raises KeyError, failing the whole batch; with Arroyo retries this becomes a poison pill blocking the partition. A defensive .get with a fallback (e.g. end_timestamp or 0) or explicit schema guarantee plus dead-letter handling is needed.

Insert-time eviction silently discards the earliest-ending spans, possibly the segment span

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN silently deletes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise with no metric, log, or downstream signal. The flushed segment is then emitted as if complete while missing spans; if an evicted span carried parent/redirect relationships, or the segment span itself is evicted for long-running roots whose children end later, flush_segments marks no span is_segment and produces a rootless segment under the wrong segment_id. The hard-coded 1000 also disagrees with SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans=1001 and ignores the configurable limit entirely.

Flush-time max_segment_spans enforcement removed without an equivalent guarantee

_load_segment_data no longer aborts segments exceeding self.max_segment_spans; it now loads and returns arbitrarily many spans (bounded only by the 10MiB byte check). The Lua cap does not fully replace this: it is hard-coded to 1000 rather than the configured value, only runs on the insert/merge path for the final set_key, and does not protect against keys created or grown outside that path (including pre-existing keys). Oversized segments that were previously skipped with a metric/error will now be produced downstream.

Redirect chain limit cut from 10000 to 1000 regresses deep segment trees

The redirect-following loop limit drops from 10000 to 1000 iterations (and the explanatory comment is deleted). For span trees deeper than 1000 redirects — previously supported up to 10k — set_span_id stops mid-chain, so the span is written to a wrong/intermediate set and the segment is split into multiple segments that flush separately with incorrect segment_ids. This is an unannounced behavioral regression unrelated to the eviction change.

No test covers eviction, score merging, or the new paginator path

All updated buffer tests use identical end_timestamp_precise values and at most 5 spans, so the headline behavior — eviction above 1000 spans, which spans are chosen for eviction, ZUNIONSTORE score handling for duplicates, and ordering by end time — is entirely untested, as is OptimizedCursorPaginator/negative offsets and the audit-log optimized branch. The regressions above (score summing, root eviction, datetime paginator crash, negative-slice crash) would all pass the current suite.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring check treats negated and mixed-type queries as error-only

_is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query contains the substring 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (which excludes errors) and mixed queries such as 'event.type:transaction OR event.type:error'. In those cases count() is replaced by sum(sample_weight), a column that is not meaningful for transactions/default events, so results will be wrong or undercounted. The check needs to use the parsed search query and only apply when the query provably restricts to error events.

Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed

_is_error_focused_query ignores the query argument passed through _get_event_stats and only inspects request.GET['query']. Callers that synthesize or modify the query (for example the dashboard split path builds '(query) AND !event.type:transaction' for the errors-only probe) therefore get eligibility decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, so genuinely error-only split queries are not upsampled unless the original GET parameter happens to contain 'event.type:error'. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility decision.

upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered on Discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform always returns True for the errors dataset, causing count() to be rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count', but the new SnQLFunction is only added to DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter in discover.py; the errors dataset config is untouched. A request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore send an unregistered function to the errors query builder and fail validation instead of returning stats. Register upsampled_count for the errors dataset (and any other dataset for which the transform is enabled) or restrict the transform to datasets that define it; the added Snuba tests never exercise dataset=errors.

sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight

The upsampled_count aggregate is a bare sum(sample_weight) wrapped in toInt64. Events in allowlisted projects that were ingested without error sampling (or before sample_weight was populated) have a NULL/0 sample_weight, so they contribute nothing and can make an entire bucket NULL/0 instead of counting once, silently under-reporting historical and unsampled errors. The aggregate should treat a missing weight as 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce/ifNull(sample_weight, 1))) so unsampled events count normally.

This adds a top-level file named 'sentry-repo' whose entire content is 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental gitlink/submodule artifact without any .gitmodules entry. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, pollutes the repository root, and can confuse tooling that scans the tree. Remove the file before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' without escaping or length-prefixing. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct triples produce the same key: for example name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both produce "..._dashboards:read_a_b_c". A denial for one resource can consequently fast-path-deny a different resource for 30 seconds. Use an unambiguous encoding such as separated, escaped, or hashed components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-based concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, causing key collisions and incorrect denial-cache hits that affect user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache key omits identity type and can poison renderer checks

The denial key is built only from namespace, raw subject UID, action, name, and parent folder, ignoring checkReq.IdentityType. Anonymous subjects and the render service both commonly use UID "0"; an anonymous denial for dashboards:read on a dashboard is therefore cached under the same key as a render-service check for that dashboard. The later render check returns Allowed:false from permDenialCache before getRendererPermissions can return its wildcard read permission, incorrectly breaking rendering for up to the 30-second denial TTL. Include the identity type (or do not denial-cache synthetic identities such as renderer) in the key.

Denials caused by the stale folder tree are cached, extending folder staleness

On a cached-permission miss Check re-queries permissions from the DB, but checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions still resolve ancestors through buildFolderTree, which returns the short-TTL cached folder tree without refreshing it. For a dashboard whose access is inherited from an ancestor above its immediate parent, a newly created/re-parented folder can therefore still produce Allowed:false, and lines 153-155 then write that result into permDenialCache. The false denial is now pinned for another denial-cache TTL even after the folder tree refreshes, partially defeating the PR's goal for newly created folders. Do not denial-cache denials that depended on the folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the DB fallback path.

Every denied check for a new resource name bypasses the permission cache to the DB

If cached permissions do not allow the requested name, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which after this PR always queries the permission store. The denial cache only helps repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent); a caller probing or enumerating many distinct dashboard/folder names—each a distinct denial key—forces a full permission DB query per name, with singleflight only deduplicating concurrent identical requests. This removes the previous cache protection against sequential negative-check DB load and needs a bound (for example revalidate at most once per cached permission-set generation/TTL window) rather than per-resource requery.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. Because the file I/O is also performed while holding the exclusive lock, a cold-cache burst in non-Dev mode serializes redundant disk reads and blocks fast-path readers instead of only the first caller loading and the rest reusing the newly cached value. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled on return

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch legacy writes in goroutines using context.WithTimeoutCause derived from the incoming request ctx. That parent context is owned by the API-server request and may be cancelled as soon as the handler returns the unified-storage result, racing with or cancelling the legacy write. The 10s timeout does not detach the goroutine from the parent. Consequently the supposedly protective legacy copy can silently never be written, especially for slower legacy stores. The legacy context should be detached (for example context.WithoutCancel/background-derived) while preserving values, with only the new timeout applied.

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the asynchronous Legacy.Create, while immediately returning `created` to the caller. The caller/serializer and the legacy store can therefore read or mutate the same underlying object concurrently (for example resource version, UID or timestamps set by a store). Update similarly shares `objInfo` with an asynchronous legacy call after the synchronous storage update has already consumed it. This is a data race and can produce corrupted or inconsistent legacy writes; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy/computed object.

Mode 3 update no longer passes the storage-computed object to legacy

Update now passes the original `objInfo` directly to Legacy.Update. A registry Update implementation recomputes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the old object it loads from legacy storage, so legacy recomputes the update against a different (possibly missing or stale) old object instead of applying the exact object already committed to unified storage, as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did. This can make the asynchronous legacy update fail (for example NotFound/conflict) or diverge from unified storage while the API call reports success. The computed/returned storage object should be wrapped and passed to legacy.

Asynchronous legacy failures are not logged

The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only feed a duration metric and discard the error otherwise. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy failures with object context. If the legacy safety copy fails in mode 3, operators have no log message identifying the kind/name/error to reconcile the divergence; only an aggregate metric counter changes. Each goroutine should log the returned error (without relying on the possibly-cancelled request logger).

Mode 3 tests never wait for or verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example Create at lines 30-32 and Update at lines 313-315) but return/assert immediately after the dual-writer call and never synchronize with the goroutine or call AssertCalled/AssertExpectations for the legacy mock. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is removed, cancelled, or never executes, and leaked goroutines can instead race with later tests using the shared mock/example objects. Tests need a synchronization/wait mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was invoked (and that failures are handled).

Mode 3 integration test synchronously asserts legacy visibility after async writes

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes through the k8s API and immediately checks the legacy playlist API (for example the legacy list/get checks inside doPlaylistTests). Because mode 3 now performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines, there is no happens-before guarantee that the legacy row exists when those assertions run. This makes the new file/unified-storage mode 3 integration cases flaky and can also hide eventual-consistency behaviour that needs polling with a timeout instead of immediate equality assertions.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback translations can be permanently cached as missing

I18n.translate only loads config.locale before consulting the LRU cache, not the fallback locales configured in config/initializers/i18n.rb. If a no-argument translation is first looked up when its fallback locale (site default or :en) has not been loaded, translate_no_cache returns a 'translation missing' string and lines 71-76 freeze and cache it under the current locale. Loading the fallback locale later does not invalidate @cache, so the missing-translation string keeps being served until LRU eviction or reload, defeating the fallback feature.

Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests

ensure_loaded! is only called from ApplicationController#set_locale. Server-side translations also happen in background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console and model code, where no controller before_filter runs. In those contexts I18n.translate loads only the current locale, so keys missing from that locale but present in the site-default or English files return 'translation missing' instead of falling back, making the feature inconsistent between requests and jobs/mailers.

FallbackLocaleList breaks the I18n.fallbacks Hash contract

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but overrides [] to ignore anything stored in the hash and always synthesize a value. Code using the documented I18n fallbacks API, e.g. I18n.fallbacks[:de] = [:fr] or the Fallbacks#map helper provided by the i18n gem/Rails, will write entries that are never read back, and enumeration/keys/empty? report an empty hash even though [] returns entries. Per-locale fallback customization is therefore silently discarded.

Every fallback lookup queries SiteSetting and crashes if it is unset

The i18n Fallbacks backend calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on each translation lookup, and this implementation calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym every time. That ties hot-path translation (including translations with arguments, which bypass the accelerator cache) to the DB-backed settings store, adds a settings lookup per translation, breaks translations performed before the database/settings are available (boot, migrations), and raises NoMethodError if default_locale is ever nil instead of degrading to :en.

No tests cover the new fallback ordering or loading behavior

The PR adds a custom FallbackLocaleList, a new I18n.ensure_loaded!, and a per-request loading hook, and removes the Rails config.i18n.fallbacks settings, but adds no specs. There is no coverage that a missing key in the user locale resolves to the site-default then English text, that duplicate locales (user == default == :en) are de-duplicated, or that fallback files are loaded in non-controller contexts, so the cache-poisoning and jobs/mailers gaps above can regress undetected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
