CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub) raises NoMethodError whenever an RSS/Atom item has no content element (SimpleRSS returns nil for missing fields, common for summary-only feeds), and String#scrub does not exist on the Ruby 1.9/2.0 runtimes this codebase targets. Because there is no per-item rescue, one such item aborts the whole hourly poll mid-loop: remaining items are never imported and the job fails on every run. The title at line 36 can likewise be nil. Guard nil fields and isolate failures per item.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: calling i.content.scrub when an RSS item lacks content raises an exception. Although it adds other concerns and recommends guarding nil fields rather than explicitly falling back to description, it directly matches the golden issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer is interpolated unescaped into a script and misused as postMessage targetOrigin

The layout embeds '<%= request.referer %>' directly inside a single-quoted JavaScript string with no escaping (no j/escape_javascript or JSON encoding). A referer containing a single quote or </script> breaks out of the string and executes attacker script in the embed page on the Discourse origin. Independently, postMessage's targetOrigin must be an origin (scheme://host:port), but a full referer URL including path is passed, so browsers will not deliver the discourse-resize message and iframe resizing silently never works.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unescaped request.referer interpolation into JavaScript and resulting XSS vulnerability. Its additional postMessage concern does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate: Imported feed/remote HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method raw_html (and the update path at line 36 does the same), and Post#cook returns raw verbatim for such posts, so cooked == raw. Neither PollFeed content nor the absolutize_urls step sanitizes the HTML: script tags, event-handler attributes (e.g. ), javascript: URLs etc. from an RSS/Atom feed item survive into the stored post and are output with `raw post.cooked` in the embed view and in normal topic rendering. Anyone who can influence a polled feed (or a page fetched via import_remote, where the PollFeed path bypasses Readability's tag whitelist entirely) gets stored XSS in the browsers of forum visitors and admins.

import_remote fetches an attacker-influenced URL with open() and no SSRF safeguards

TopicRetriever only compares URI(embed_url).host to embeddable_host, then TopicEmbed.import_remote does open(url).read with no timeout, size limit, or redirect control. open-uri follows redirects, so a URL on the allowed host that redirects to an internal address (e.g. 169.254.169.254 or localhost admin endpoints) bypasses the host check and the server fetches internal content (SSRF); a slow or huge response also ties up the Sidekiq worker indefinitely. Fetching should re-validate the host after redirects, block private/link-local addresses, and set open/read timeouts and a size cap.

Every request for an unknown embed_url enqueues a new retrieve job

When no TopicEmbed exists, each GET /embed/best enqueues another Jobs::RetrieveTopic, and the loading page auto-reloads every 30 seconds, so a single embedded page (or a bot hitting the endpoint with rotating embed_url values, needing only a matching Referer) can flood Sidekiq with jobs and outbound fetches. The 60-second throttle lives inside TopicRetriever at job-execution time, so it does not stop unbounded enqueueing. Deduplicate/throttle at enqueue time (e.g. a redis setnx keyed by embed_url before Jobs.enqueue).

Check-then-create race on embed_url despite the unique index

import does TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first and only creates the embed inside the transaction when blank, but topic_embeds has a unique index on embed_url. Two concurrent executions (hourly PollFeed overlapping a RetrieveTopic job for the same URL, or two retrieve jobs) can both see no embed, both create a topic/post via PostCreator, and then one raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique on TopicEmbed.create!, rolling back and failing the job after side effects such as job enqueues from post creation. The create path needs to rescue RecordNotUnique and reload the winning embed, or serialize import per URL.

Embed controller spec expects synchronous TopicRetriever but controller enqueues a job

The 'tells the topic retriever to work' example stubs TopicRetriever.new and expects retrieve to be called, but EmbedController#best never references TopicRetriever; it calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). As written the mocha expectation is never satisfied and this example fails, so the PR's own test suite is red and the actual enqueued-args behaviour (user_id, embed_url) is untested. Update the spec to expect Jobs.enqueue with :retrieve_topic and the right arguments.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overrides the existing five-argument version

Ruby does not support method overloading. Defining self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) at line 149 replaces self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) at line 145, making the latter dead code. Any existing caller passing separate width and height will now raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments, 5 for 4) instead of resizing. The old signature must be preserved or all its callers migrated, e.g. by handling both a String dimension and width/height in one method.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the second downsize definition overrides the original width/height version, making it unreachable and breaking existing callers that pass separate dimensions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores site settings and upload type

validateUploadedFile previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments each respected the admin-configured limit. Replacing it with a fixed 10 * 1024 makes the client accept files above a site's configured max_image_size_kb/max_attachment_size_kb (attachments are not downsized server-side at all, and images still exceeding the limit after five reductions are rejected by the server with a confusing error after upload), and rejects nothing for sites that configured a limit above 10 MB. The same hardcoding in the 413 handler at line 246 also reports a wrong max_size_kb in the error message for such sites.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the hardcoded 10 * 1024 limit replacing per-type site settings, causing client/server limit divergence and incorrect size reporting in the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIFs cannot be downsized with a percentage dimension

The controller passes "80%" to OptimizedImage.downsize with allow_animation taken from SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When animation is allowed, OptimizedImage.optimize routes GIFs to downsize_instructions_animated/resize_instructions_animated, which passes the dimension to `gifsicle --resize-fit`; gifsicle expects a WIDTHxHEIGHT geometry, not "80%", so it fails and the GIF is never reduced. When animation is not allowed, the non-animated path uses `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame and silently flattens an animated upload into a static image. Either way animated GIF uploads are broken by this feature.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: when animated thumbnails are allowed, passing "80%" reaches gifsicle --resize-fit, which requires WxH geometry, causing GIF downsizing to fail. The additional claim about flattening when animation is disabled does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize result is ignored while converting a file onto itself

OptimizedImage.downsize is invoked with tempfile.path as both input and output and its boolean return value is discarded. convert_with returns false on a failed ImageMagick/gifsicle/ImageOptim run, and an in-place convert that fails or is interrupted can leave the target truncated or partially written. The loop then retries up to five times on that possibly-corrupt file and create_upload proceeds to Upload.create_for with it, so a transient conversion failure turns a valid upload into a corrupt stored file instead of keeping the original or reporting an error.

Synchronous downsizing loop enables expensive processing of huge/decompression-bomb images

The change raises the accepted image size to 10 MB (line 55 for URL downloads and the JS limit) and then runs up to five full ImageMagick convert plus ImageOptim passes over the file inside the request/deferred upload job, gated only on compressed file size. A small compressed file can decode to enormous pixel dimensions, so each pass can consume very large CPU/memory, and an attacker can repeat this per upload. There is no pixel-dimension bound or timeout before invoking convert, creating an image-bomb denial-of-service vector that did not exist with the previous size gate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicUser.find_by can return nil for a logged-in user who has no topic_users row for this topic (for example, opening the emailed link in a different browser/session where no row was ever created, or after the row was removed). Line 107 immediately calls tu.notification_level, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. Use TopicUser.change (which creates the row when missing) or otherwise handle the nil case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: TopicUser.find_by may return nil when no record exists, and calling tu.notification_level without a nil check causes a crash.

false_positives.candidate:
State-changing unsubscribe is performed by a plain GET request

The unsubscribe action is routed as GET (config/routes.rb lines 440-441) and mutates notification_level on every request. Email link scanners, antivirus prefetchers, browser prefetch, and simply reloading the page will therefore change the user's notification state without any intentional confirmation click. A mail security gateway that follows links can silently mute topics for users who never clicked anything.

Unsubscribe is not idempotent and does not actually mute on first click

Each visit steps the level down exactly one notch: watching/tracking becomes regular, and only a second visit (or a refresh of the landing page) becomes muted. So the first click on the email link leaves the user at regular — still notified of mentions/quotes/replies to their posts — while the landing page claims 'You will stop receiving notifications', and a refresh unexpectedly changes state again. The action should set a single deterministic target level (muted) in one idempotent operation.

Direct save! bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

Mutating tu.notification_level and calling save! bypasses TopicUser.change, which is the canonical path used by set_notifications: it stamps notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, publishes a MessageBus /topic/:id notification_level_change message, and runs observe_after_save_callbacks_for. As written, already-open clients keep showing the old notification level and downstream observers/audit data are never updated.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url for every unsubscribe email

config/locales/server.en.yml changes the shared unsubscribe_link string to interpolate %{unsubscribe_url}, and MessageBuilder#body (line 90) and #html_part (line 67) render that string for any message built with add_unsubscribe_link: true. Only UserNotifications#send_notification_email was updated to pass unsubscribe_url; any other current or future caller that sets add_unsubscribe_link without unsubscribe_url will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to deliver mail entirely, instead of simply omitting the per-topic sentence. The per-topic line should be conditional on unsubscribe_url being present.

Ember route/controller/template names for unsubscribe do not match

The route is registered as top-level 'topicUnsubscribe' (with controller controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6 and view views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, i.e. topic-unsubscribe), but the template is placed at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which is the name for a nested topic.unsubscribe route. Ember's resolver will look for a topic-unsubscribe template for this route and find none, so the unsubscribe landing page renders empty/without the notification-state controls even though the server-side mutation already happened.

No test covers the new unsubscribe behavior end-to-end

The only spec change adds unsubscribe_url to an existing fixture but adds no assertion that the per-topic URL appears in the body/HTML, and there are no controller specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe at all (missing TopicUser row, watching vs regular vs muted starting levels, slug redirect, JSON vs HTML). The nil-row crash and the one-notch-at-a-time behavior above would both have been caught by such specs.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Tunnel script is macOS-only and silently reports failure as success

Line 68 uses BSD/macOS syntax `sed -i '' -E ...`, which fails under GNU sed on Linux ('' is treated as an input file), so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated there. Additionally, the failure paths at lines 46-58 call cleanup(), which unconditionally `exit 0`, so rate-limit and 'failed to extract URL' failures are reported to callers/CI as success. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same portability bug: BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` syntax fails with GNU sed on Linux. The additional concerns do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws a generic Error instead of a tRPC error and has no tests

When the credential does not belong to the user the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`, which tRPC surfaces as an opaque INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) rather than a NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN client error, so the client can only show the generic 'Error deleting cache' toast and monitoring records a server fault for a routine authorization denial. The new mutation also ships without any test covering the ownership check or the deletion, so a future refactor could allow deleting another user's cache (prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany is keyed only by the input credentialId) without failing CI.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: throwing a generic Error for an authorization failure causes tRPC to return INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) instead of a structured TRPCError with an appropriate client-error code such as FORBIDDEN. The additional testing concern does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US locale

The timestamp is formatted with new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...) regardless of the user's configured locale obtained via useLocale. Non-English users will see US-style dates (e.g. 7/15/25) mixed into an otherwise localized UI; the formatter should use the active locale (and ideally be memoized rather than constructed on every render).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same localization issue: the date formatter hardcodes en-US instead of using the user's locale from useLocale. The additional memoization suggestion does not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

The deleteCache mutation only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess callback, unlike disconnectMutation below it which invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations on settle. SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper passes onChanged which may be undefined, so after a successful deletion the connectedCalendars query is not refetched, cacheUpdatedAt remains truthy, and the dropdown continues to show 'Cache Status' and 'Delete cached data' for cache that no longer exists until a manual reload.

Cache status includes expired cache entries

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups all CalendarCache rows for the credentials without filtering on expiresAt, whereas getCachedAvailability only serves rows with expiresAt >= now. After the one-month caching period expires, the UI will still report a 'Last updated' cache status and offer 'Delete cached data' for an entry that is never actually served, misleading users and support about whether cached availability is in effect.

dev:cron depends on undeclared tsx fetched via npx

The script was changed from ts-node (a declared devDependency) to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but tsx is not declared in this package's dependencies/devDependencies. In this Yarn-workspaces repo the command will attempt to download an unpinned tsx from the network at runtime, failing offline and introducing an unreviewed, unpinned executable into the dev workflow; tsx should be added as a pinned devDependency or the ts-node runner retained.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check never checks the slot end time

Both start and end are computed identically from slotStartTime (hour*60+minute); slotEndTime is never used. A slot that starts inside working hours but ends after workingHour.endTime (e.g. a 60-minute event starting 30 minutes before the end of availability) therefore passes the check and is offered outside the host's working hours.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the end time is incorrectly computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, causing the working-hours check to miss slots that end outside availability.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date override comparison uses object identity

dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) compares two distinct Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false. The intended special case for an empty override (start equals end, i.e. unavailable all day) is therefore never detected via this branch and relies on accidental fall-through of the surrounding comparisons, so empty overrides are not reliably honoured.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === to compare separately created Dayjs objects compares references rather than date values, causing the equality check to return false.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override slots bypass busy-time checks

When a slot's day matches a date override, checkIfIsAvailable returns true at line 133-135 before reaching the busy.every(...) check at the end of the function. Consequently a fixed or round-robin host who has a date override but also has a conflicting Cal booking or connected-calendar event during the override window is still reported as available, allowing double bookings on override days.

Working-hours find logic rejects valid split shifts and accepts days with no availability

The code uses workingHours.find(...) and returns unavailable if ANY entry for that weekday is outside the slot. With split/multiple working-hour ranges on the same day, a slot valid in the second range is rejected because it is outside the first. Conversely, if no entry includes slotStartTime.day(), find returns undefined and execution falls through to the busy check, so a host with no working hours that day is treated as available — defeating the per-fixed-host check this PR adds, since getTimeSlots only receives aggregated hours.

Multiple date overrides on the same day are handled incorrectly

dateOverrides.find(...) stops at the first override for which the callback returns true, and the callback returns true when the slot is OUTSIDE that override. With two override ranges on the same day, a slot inside the first range but outside the second makes find succeed and the function returns false, incorrectly hiding slots that are inside one of the day's overrides.

Override conversion assumes timeZone is present and loses day overflow

override.timeZone is optional in the TimeRange type (packages/types/schedule.d.ts), but line 212-213 unconditionally calls .tz(override.timeZone); callers passing overrides without timeZone get a guessed/default timezone offset and wrong slots. Additionally startTime/endTime are reduced to hour*60+minute after adding the offset, so an override pushed past midnight by the offset wraps to a small minute value, producing endTime <= startTime which buildSlots discards (start >= end), causing override availability near midnight in another timezone to disappear rather than appear on the correct invitee day.

No test for the round-robin fixed-host date override fix

The PR description states the main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides constrain round-robin events, but the only added test exercises a personal event in a different invitee timezone. There is no scenario with schedulingType ROUND_ROBIN, a fixed host with a date override, and a loose host, verifying that slots outside the fixed host's override are hidden and slots inside it remain — so the new checkIfIsAvailable fixed-host path (including its busy-time and working-hours behaviour) is untested and regressions would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count is written from a stale read instead of an atomic increment

Both retry writes set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read at the start of the run. If two cron invocations overlap, both read the same retryCount (e.g. 1), both fail, and both write 2's predecessor value 2-minus-one (i.e. both write 2 when starting from 1 is fine, but starting from 0 both write 1), so failed attempts are under-counted and the `retryCount > 1` deletion threshold can be postponed indefinitely under repeated overlap. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` update instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same concurrency bug: updating retryCount from a stale reminder.retryCount value can lose increments. Both cover the two retry updates and recommend Prisma's atomic increment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-count deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The second OR branch matches only `retryCount > 1` and does not require `method: SMS`, `scheduled: false`, or a future/past scheduledDate. This SMS cron therefore deletes EMAIL and WHATSAPP WorkflowReminder rows as well whenever their retryCount exceeds 1, even though it never attempted to schedule them and their own handlers may still need them. The retry cleanup should be restricted to the unscheduled SMS reminders this job actually retries.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion branch, which causes non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp to be deleted. The candidate's additional scoping suggestions do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Retry-count update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update` without its own error handling. If that update fails — for example the row was deleted by a concurrent cron invocation (Prisma P2025) or the original error was a transient database failure — the new exception escapes the catch, terminates the for loop, and the handler returns an error instead of processing the remaining unscheduled reminders. One bad reminder can therefore block all later reminders in the run; the increment should be best-effort or use a delete/updateMany that tolerates a missing row.

Reminders with no recipient or no message never get a retry count

Retry counting only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` (via the scheduledSMS-null branch) or in the catch block. A reminder whose booking has no `smsReminderNumber`, whose workflow step has no `sendTo`, or whose message resolves to empty silently falls through with retryCount unchanged and `scheduled` still false, so it is re-fetched and re-processed on every cron invocation until its scheduledDate finally passes — exactly the endless-rescheduling loop this PR is meant to eliminate for undeliverable SMS reminders.

Public findMany method removed without migrating callers

The conversion deletes InsightsBookingService.findMany, which previously accepted BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs and executed the query, and replaces it with getBaseConditions that only returns a Prisma.Sql fragment. No caller in this PR is updated to construct and execute a $queryRaw query instead. Any existing consumer calling service.findMany(...) will now fail TypeScript compilation (and would fail at runtime if untyped), breaking the insights data path until every call site is migrated.

Event-type filter returns an unparenthesized OR expression

buildFilterConditions stores the event-type condition as `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` with no parentheses around the whole OR, and when it is the only filter getFilterConditions returns that fragment unchanged. getBaseConditions happens to wrap it, but the public getFilterConditions result is unsafe to interpolate into a larger WHERE clause: `WHERE "userId" = 1 OR "eventParentId" = 2 AND <other>` is parsed by PostgreSQL as `"userId" = 1 OR ("eventParentId" = 2 AND <other>)` because AND binds tighter than OR, so rows can be returned that ignore the additional constraints. The previous structured Prisma where-object preserved this grouping automatically. The fragment should be wrapped as `((...) OR (...))` at construction.

Multi-branch authorization conditions are not wrapped as a single expression

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition reduce their branches to `(<branch A>) OR (<branch B>)` without enclosing the complete OR in parentheses, and the single-branch case returns a bare AND expression. getBaseConditions wraps the result, but the public getAuthorizationConditions result loses the grouping guarantee the old Prisma where-object provided: a caller interpolating it as `WHERE ${auth} AND <date/status condition>` gets `branchA OR (branchB AND <condition>)`, so branch A rows bypass the caller's date/status restrictions. This is an authorization-adjacent correctness risk; the builders should return a fully parenthesized expression.

Org and team raw SQL is never actually executed against the database

The org/team authorization tests only compare the returned Prisma.Sql object with an expected Prisma.Sql built from the same template syntax, and the sole $queryRaw execution test at line 481 exercises only the user scope. Consequently invalid PostgreSQL produced for org/team scopes — for example the `= ANY(${array})` parameter binding on lines 333-343 of the test / in the service, quoted identifiers, or boolean comparisons — would pass these tests and only fail (or misbehave) when a real org/team insights query runs. At least one org-scope and one team-scope test should execute the conditions via $queryRaw against the seeded data and assert the returned booking ids, especially since the PR description states the tests were not successfully run during development.

Caching coverage deleted while caching logic remains

This PR removes the entire 'Caching' describe block that verified repeated getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions calls return cached results, but the service still implements that caching (cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions in insightsBooking.ts). No replacement test covers it, so a regression that removes or breaks the cache — causing repeated membership/team database lookups on every insights query — would go undetected. The caching tests should have been ported to Prisma.Sql expectations like the other tests instead of deleted.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is replaced with literal string "refresh_token"

When the parsed response has no `refresh_token` (always the case in sharing mode because the schema strips it, and possible in normal mode where it is optional), this line sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers such as Zoom and Webex copy that value into the stored credential key, so the database now contains a bogus refresh token and any later non-synced refresh will fail with invalid_grant.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", resulting in an invalid stored token that breaks subsequent refreshes and authentication.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore commit past a message whose processing failed, so it will never be retried or sent to a DLQ. This directly contradicts the strategy docstring claiming it only commits offsets after successful processing and can silently lose uptime results.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected when workers fall behind. Arroyo will keep submitting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them, accumulating decoded WorkItems (including the original Kafka message) in memory indefinitely, growing OffsetTracker sets for uncommittable partitions as well. A slow subscription or downstream outage therefore risks OOM and massive reprocessing on restart rather than natural backpressure as claimed in the class docstring.

Shared queue pool is destroyed by the first strategy close and reused after rebalance

The FixedQueuePool (and its worker threads and OffsetTracker) is created once on the factory and handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo creates/closes strategies on partition assignment and rebalance; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down that shared pool, and queue.Queue.put() on a shut-down queue raises ShutDown. The next assignment reuses the same dead pool (factory only nulls it in factory.shutdown(), not on strategy close), so subsequent messages fail to enqueue, are swallowed by submit()'s broad except handler, and are marked complete without processing. The shared OffsetTracker also retains last_committed across assignments, so a partition reassigned at a lower offset can never be committed again.

Close stops committing before queued work is drained

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, and it never waits for queues to empty. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so a worker that finishes its current item exits at the loop condition instead of draining remaining queued items. Consequently queued items are abandoned on graceful shutdown and any items workers do finish after the commit thread stops never have their offsets committed, causing avoidable duplicate reprocessing and violating the graceful-shutdown expectation.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() on a string group key. For strings, hash() is randomized per interpreter process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the same subscription maps to different queues in different processes and across restarts. That breaks the documented consistent-assignment/ordering guarantee whenever work for a group moves between consumer processes or the consumer restarts, and makes distribution non-reproducible; a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5, as used elsewhere in the uptime consumer) should be used instead.

Submit swallows grouping/decoder failures and marks the offset complete

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one broad except that logs the error and then add_offset()+complete_offset()s the message. Any failure in grouping_fn (or an enqueue failure such as a shut-down queue) therefore makes the message eligible for offset commit even though it was never processed, silently dropping it instead of surfacing the failure to Arroyo for retry/DLQ handling.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing crashes Django querysets and is not a permission-safe feature

When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset is negative, this passes a negative start to queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django querysets explicitly raise AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so the advertised advanced pagination path crashes rather than paginating. The same problem remains in BasePaginator.get_result at line 182 for is_prev cursors. The comments claiming the ORM handles this and that queryset-level permissions make it safe are false; cursors are user-controlled via the cursor query parameter.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: when enable_advanced_features is True, a negative cursor.offset is passed directly as the start of the queryset slice. The candidate adds detail about Django raising an error on negative indexing and about cursors being user-controlled, but the core issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing crashes Django querysets and is not a permission-safe feature

The same problem remains in BasePaginator.get_result at line 182 for is_prev cursors. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says the same negative-offset problem exists in BasePaginator.get_result for is_prev cursors, where negative offsets reach queryset slicing. That is the golden issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime ordering it is used with

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil directly on getattr(item, self.key) and value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value. The only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, uses order_by='-datetime', so get_item_key receives a datetime and raises TypeError, and build_queryset would compare a datetime column against an integer cursor value. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes via timestamps. Any superuser/global-access user requesting optimized_pagination=true will get a 500 instead of audit logs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate names the same bug as the golden comment. get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime key from order_by='-datetime', which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM, corrupting scores of spans present in both sets

Both zunionstore calls omit AGGREGATE/WEIGHTS, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both the destination and source sorted sets. A span payload already in set_key that is also in span_key/parent_key (duplicate delivery or overlapping merge) gets its end_timestamp_precise roughly doubled, moving it to ~year 2077. That corrupts the ordering used by ZPOPMIN eviction: duplicated spans become effectively unevictable while legitimate spans are evicted instead. The old SUNIONSTORE had no such side effect; AGGREGATE MAX (or equivalent) is required.

Set-to-sorted-set conversion breaks on all pre-existing Redis buffer keys

process_spans now ZADDs into span-buf:s:* keys that existing deployments hold as Redis SETs (previously SADD), and the Lua script and _load_segment_data now use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN on them. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these commands on set-typed keys, so every in-flight segment buffered before deploy will fail processing/flushing until its TTL (up to redis_ttl, 3600s) expires, stalling or erroring batches. There is no key versioning, migration, or type check in the PR.

New required Span field inserted before a defaulted field breaks existing constructors

end_timestamp_precise is added as a required positional field immediately before is_segment_span, which previously was the seventh positional/keyword field with a default. Any Span(...) construction elsewhere (other consumers, scripts, tests not in this diff) that omits the new field now raises TypeError, and any construction passing is_segment_span positionally will silently assign a bool as end_timestamp_precise, which then becomes a Redis sorted-set score of 0/1. Adding it at the end with a default, or updating all call sites verifiably, is needed.

Direct indexing of end_timestamp_precise turns a missing field into a poison-pill batch

process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] for every Kafka message. Previously this field was not read, and the updated tests themselves show messages legitimately lacking it before this change. A single span without the field raises KeyError, failing the whole batch; with Arroyo retries this becomes a poison pill blocking the partition. A defensive .get with a fallback (e.g. end_timestamp or 0) or explicit schema guarantee plus dead-letter handling is needed.

Insert-time eviction silently discards the earliest-ending spans, possibly the segment span

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN silently deletes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise with no metric, log, or downstream signal. The flushed segment is then emitted as if complete while missing spans; if an evicted span carried parent/redirect relationships, or the segment span itself is evicted for long-running roots whose children end later, flush_segments marks no span is_segment and produces a rootless segment under the wrong segment_id. The hard-coded 1000 also disagrees with SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans=1001 and ignores the configurable limit entirely.

Flush-time max_segment_spans enforcement removed without an equivalent guarantee

_load_segment_data no longer aborts segments exceeding self.max_segment_spans; it now loads and returns arbitrarily many spans (bounded only by the 10MiB byte check). The Lua cap does not fully replace this: it is hard-coded to 1000 rather than the configured value, only runs on the insert/merge path for the final set_key, and does not protect against keys created or grown outside that path (including pre-existing keys). Oversized segments that were previously skipped with a metric/error will now be produced downstream.

Redirect chain limit cut from 10000 to 1000 regresses deep segment trees

The redirect-following loop limit drops from 10000 to 1000 iterations (and the explanatory comment is deleted). For span trees deeper than 1000 redirects — previously supported up to 10k — set_span_id stops mid-chain, so the span is written to a wrong/intermediate set and the segment is split into multiple segments that flush separately with incorrect segment_ids. This is an unannounced behavioral regression unrelated to the eviction change.

No test covers eviction, score merging, or the new paginator path

All updated buffer tests use identical end_timestamp_precise values and at most 5 spans, so the headline behavior — eviction above 1000 spans, which spans are chosen for eviction, ZUNIONSTORE score handling for duplicates, and ordering by end time — is entirely untested, as is OptimizedCursorPaginator/negative offsets and the audit-log optimized branch. The regressions above (score summing, root eviction, datetime paginator crash, negative-slice crash) would all pass the current suite.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which can differ from the closure dataset during dashboard discover-split handling (e.g. an errors-only call is made with discover while the outer dataset is metrics/discover, or vice versa). is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is nevertheless passed the outer dataset, so eligibility is decided for the wrong dataset: error split results can miss upsampling and transaction/metrics split results can be decided from the wrong dataset context. Pass scoped_dataset to the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check is passed the outer dataset when it should use scoped_dataset, so upsampling can be skipped in dashboard split paths. The candidate also proposes passing scoped_dataset as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring check treats negated and mixed-type queries as error-only

_is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query contains the substring 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (which excludes errors) and mixed queries such as 'event.type:transaction OR event.type:error'. In those cases count() is replaced by sum(sample_weight), a column that is not meaningful for transactions/default events, so results will be wrong or undercounted. The check needs to use the parsed search query and only apply when the query provably restricts to error events.

Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed

_is_error_focused_query ignores the query argument passed through _get_event_stats and only inspects request.GET['query']. Callers that synthesize or modify the query (for example the dashboard split path builds '(query) AND !event.type:transaction' for the errors-only probe) therefore get eligibility decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, so genuinely error-only split queries are not upsampled unless the original GET parameter happens to contain 'event.type:error'. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility decision.

upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered on Discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform always returns True for the errors dataset, causing count() to be rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count', but the new SnQLFunction is only added to DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter in discover.py; the errors dataset config is untouched. A request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore send an unregistered function to the errors query builder and fail validation instead of returning stats. Register upsampled_count for the errors dataset (and any other dataset for which the transform is enabled) or restrict the transform to datasets that define it; the added Snuba tests never exercise dataset=errors.

sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight

The upsampled_count aggregate is a bare sum(sample_weight) wrapped in toInt64. Events in allowlisted projects that were ingested without error sampling (or before sample_weight was populated) have a NULL/0 sample_weight, so they contribute nothing and can make an entire bucket NULL/0 instead of counting once, silently under-reporting historical and unsampled errors. The aggregate should treat a missing weight as 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce/ifNull(sample_weight, 1))) so unsampled events count normally.

Stray nested-repository pointer file committed

This adds a top-level file named 'sentry-repo' whose entire content is 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental gitlink/submodule artifact without any .gitmodules entry. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, pollutes the repository root, and can confuse tooling that scans the tree. Remove the file before merging.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' without escaping or length-prefixing. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct triples produce the same key: for example name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both produce "..._dashboards:read_a_b_c". A denial for one resource can consequently fast-path-deny a different resource for 30 seconds. Use an unambiguous encoding such as separated, escaped, or hashed components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: userPermDenialCacheKey joins its components with underscores and no escaping, so keys can collide and cause incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache key omits identity type and can poison renderer checks

The denial key is built only from namespace, raw subject UID, action, name, and parent folder, ignoring checkReq.IdentityType. Anonymous subjects and the render service both commonly use UID "0"; an anonymous denial for dashboards:read on a dashboard is therefore cached under the same key as a render-service check for that dashboard. The later render check returns Allowed:false from permDenialCache before getRendererPermissions can return its wildcard read permission, incorrectly breaking rendering for up to the 30-second denial TTL. Include the identity type (or do not denial-cache synthetic identities such as renderer) in the key.

Denials caused by the stale folder tree are cached, extending folder staleness

On a cached-permission miss Check re-queries permissions from the DB, but checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions still resolve ancestors through buildFolderTree, which returns the short-TTL cached folder tree without refreshing it. For a dashboard whose access is inherited from an ancestor above its immediate parent, a newly created/re-parented folder can therefore still produce Allowed:false, and lines 153-155 then write that result into permDenialCache. The false denial is now pinned for another denial-cache TTL even after the folder tree refreshes, partially defeating the PR's goal for newly created folders. Do not denial-cache denials that depended on the folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the DB fallback path.

Every denied check for a new resource name bypasses the permission cache to the DB

If cached permissions do not allow the requested name, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which after this PR always queries the permission store. The denial cache only helps repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent); a caller probing or enumerating many distinct dashboard/folder names—each a distinct denial key—forces a full permission DB query per name, with singleflight only deduplicating concurrent identical requests. This removes the previous cache protection against sequential negative-check DB load and needs a bound (for example revalidate at most once per cached permission-set generation/TTL window) rather than per-resource requery.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender check crashes for integrations without sender metadata

integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes every pre-existing Integration has metadata['sender'] as a dict with 'login'. Integrations created through the normal pipeline do not guarantee this: build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] when state.get('sender') is present, and no pipeline view binds 'sender', so pipeline-created integrations lack it. If such an integration later exists without an OrganizationIntegration (e.g. removed from one org and reinstalled on another), this line raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of the friendly installation-failed page or a successful reinstall.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is accessed without checking that the 'sender' key exists, so integrations created without sender metadata raise a KeyError.

false_positives.candidate:
Authenticated-user check is bypassed when Integration row does not yet exist

When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state 'github_authenticated_user' to the installer. The sender check at lines 500-505 therefore only runs if the installation webhook has already created the Integration row. An attacker who knows/guesses a predictable GitHub installation_id and starts the claim flow before the webhook is processed (or where the webhook never creates the row) can complete installation as any authenticated GitHub user, defeating the validation this PR is meant to add; build_integration fetches only account info, not the installing user, so no later check compensates.

Token exchange and user-info calls can raise unhandled exceptions

safe_urlopen at line 423 is outside the try/except (which only covers safe_urlread/parse at lines 425-429), and get_user_info(payload['access_token']) at line 434 is also unguarded. A network error, TLS error, or non-2xx/invalid response from GitHub's /user endpoint will propagate as an unhandled 500 instead of rendering the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page described in the PR for bad/reused codes and verification failures.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path

The rewritten test first requests setup with only installation_id, which now just redirects into the new OAuthLoginView, and then requests setup with a deliberately wrong state value, so it fails at the state-signature check in OAuthLoginView before build_integration/get_installation_info is ever reached. The assertion for 'Invalid installation request.' therefore passes even if the GitHub 404 handling in build_integration is broken, leaving that behavior untested under the new flow.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes a literal "alias" provider instead of the created providers

Both cleanup registrations in testCacheIDPForLogin use testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") rather than the alias of the provider just created ("idp-alias-" + i, and similarly at line 425). The cleanup therefore targets a non-existent provider and the 20+ identity providers created by the test are left behind in the shared test realm, making the test suite order-dependent and potentially polluting other cache/count assertions; the cleanup should capture the per-iteration alias.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug as the golden comment. The cleanup uses the literal "alias" instead of "idp-alias-" + i.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin cache ignores organization-level invalidations

The login cache is keyed only by realm and FetchMode and getForLogin only checks isInvalid(cacheKey). Unlike getByOrganization (which also checks isInvalid(orgId)), it never checks whether the requested organizationId has been invalidated. Organization-side changes that register an invalidation for the organization id (organization update/removal and broker association changes performed through the organization provider rather than through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.create/update/remove) therefore do not evict the cached realm+mode IdentityProviderListQuery. The cached ID set keeps being served until an unrelated IdP mutation invalidates the login key, so brokers can remain visible for an organization they no longer belong to, or remain missing after being linked, on login pages.

getLoginPredicate can NPE on identity providers with a null config map

The new predicate unconditionally calls idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) for every org-linked identity provider. IdentityProviderModel allows the config to be set to null (e.g. models built/imported from representations without config), so evaluating this predicate during the new create/update/remove invalidation in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider will throw NullPointerException and fail the whole IdP operation, whereas the previous predicate only inspected enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin. The config access needs a null guard (treat missing config as not public).

Cached getForLogin loses the delegate's result ordering

On a cache hit the method collects the cached internal IDs into a HashSet and returns identityProviders.stream(), so the order of the returned stream is hash iteration order of UUID strings instead of the order produced by the JPA delegate (which getAllStream returns in its deterministic query order). Any caller of getForLogin that does not explicitly re-sort (the login bean does, but the storage provider contract gives no sorting guarantee to other callers) will now see identity providers in a different, unstable order than before this caching was added.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false through inverted dead logic

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), returns false when that value is true, and also returns false when it is false. The feature flag therefore has no effect and the branching is misleading: a maintainer trying to re-enable SQL expressions by restoring the flag check can easily invert the logic and either keep the feature permanently disabled or accidentally enable the unsafe DuckDB path. The helper should directly express the intended temporary disable (return false with a clear comment) or correctly return the flag value once the stub is removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say enableSqlExpressions always returns false because of flawed or inverted logic, which disables the feature unconditionally. They describe the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No tests cover SQL-expression rejection and existing SQL tests are not updated

The PR disables SQL expressions in ReadQuery and stubs pkg/expr/sql.DB so TablesList, RunCommands, and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', but it adds no test asserting that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, and it does not update or skip the pre-existing tests that exercise TablesList/SQLCommand execution against DuckDB. Those existing tests will now fail against the stub, while the security-critical rejection path itself remains unprotected against regression. Add a reader test for the disabled SQL type and skip/remove/update the DuckDB-dependent tests accordingly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate names the same stubbed DB methods (TablesList, RunCommands, QueryFramesInto) returning 'not implemented'. Its main framing is test coverage, but it also says existing tests will fail against the stub, which is the consequence of the same stubbed implementation. That is close enough to count as a semantic match.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command entry point is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand still accepts SQL expressions and calls NewSQLCommand without any feature-flag or disabled-feature check. It is only blocked incidentally because sql.TablesList now calls the stub DB and errors, producing a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. This leaves two different disable behaviours for SQL expressions (explicit rejection in ExpressionQueryReader versus an incidental parsing failure here), and if the stub DB's RunCommands/TablesList is ever partially restored this legacy path would again create executable SQLCommands without passing through the reader's guard. The legacy unmarshalling path should reject QueryTypeSQL explicitly as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

After the initial RLock check misses, every concurrent caller waits for the write lock and then unconditionally reloads assets-manifest.json and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache, even if another goroutine populated the cache while it was waiting. Because the file I/O is also performed while holding the exclusive lock, a cold-cache burst in non-Dev mode serializes redundant disk reads and blocks fast-path readers instead of only the first caller loading and the rest reusing the newly cached value. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring Lock (when cfg.Env != Dev) and return it if non-nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the cache is not re-checked after the write lock is acquired, so the double-checked locking is incomplete. The candidate describes this exact gap, explains its consequences, and proposes the recheck as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix

This change adds synchronization around the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, so the original race would not be reproduced or guarded against in CI (including with the race detector). A test should exercise parallel GetWebAssets calls on a cold cache (and, if feasible, in Dev mode where the cache is rewritten) against a temporary assets-manifest.json so a missing or incorrectly scoped lock fails under -race.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch at Error level (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including on success paths where err is nil, and they include the complete ids slice and SQL condition. With the configured batch size this can dump tens of thousands of IDs into error logs once per batch until cleanup finishes, creating false error alerts/on-call noise, high log volume and serialization cost, and obscuring real failures. These progress messages should be Debug (or Info without the ID list), with Error reserved for the returned error path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that routine or debugging information is logged at Error level, which pollutes the error logs. Both suggest using Debug or Info instead. The candidate matches the golden comment and adds more detail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs

The ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but this ticker drives CleanUpService.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history), not just annotation cleanup. Nothing in the PR description justifies a 10x increase in frequency for all of these jobs. This will increase database and filesystem load on every Grafana instance and shorten the effective timeout/interference window between full cleanup passes; it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or scoped/justified separately.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same change: the cleanup ticker going from 10 minutes to 1 minute. Both say this raises database load. The candidate adds detail about which jobs the ticker affects, but the underlying concern is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite and keys off configured batch size

deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when the database is SQLite and cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; otherwise it emits one '?' placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL also have bind-parameter limits (65535), so a user who raises annotation_cleanupjob_batchsize above that (the new test itself encourages very large batches such as 32767) will now get 'too many parameters' failures from the DELETE and cleanup will error on every cycle, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no host-parameter limit. The guard should be based on len(ids) and the actual dialect's parameter limit, chunking or inlining as needed per database.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) for elapsed storage time; Update does the same on storage failure (line 129). Delete records a successful storage duration using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label (line 106), creating wrong/high-cardinality series. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration (line 166). Dashboards/alerts based on these metrics will attribute failures and latency to the wrong backend and cannot be used to verify mode 3 legacy health.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says Delete records a metric using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label. That is the same issue as the golden comment, and the candidate bundles it with other metric problems.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled on return

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch legacy writes in goroutines using context.WithTimeoutCause derived from the incoming request ctx. That parent context is owned by the API-server request and may be cancelled as soon as the handler returns the unified-storage result, racing with or cancelling the legacy write. The 10s timeout does not detach the goroutine from the parent. Consequently the supposedly protective legacy copy can silently never be written, especially for slower legacy stores. The legacy context should be detached (for example context.WithoutCancel/background-derived) while preserving values, with only the new timeout applied.

Legacy goroutines race with the caller on the shared object

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the asynchronous Legacy.Create, while immediately returning `created` to the caller. The caller/serializer and the legacy store can therefore read or mutate the same underlying object concurrently (for example resource version, UID or timestamps set by a store). Update similarly shares `objInfo` with an asynchronous legacy call after the synchronous storage update has already consumed it. This is a data race and can produce corrupted or inconsistent legacy writes; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy/computed object.

Mode 3 update no longer passes the storage-computed object to legacy

Update now passes the original `objInfo` directly to Legacy.Update. A registry Update implementation recomputes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the old object it loads from legacy storage, so legacy recomputes the update against a different (possibly missing or stale) old object instead of applying the exact object already committed to unified storage, as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did. This can make the asynchronous legacy update fail (for example NotFound/conflict) or diverge from unified storage while the API call reports success. The computed/returned storage object should be wrapped and passed to legacy.

Asynchronous legacy failures are not logged

The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only feed a duration metric and discard the error otherwise. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy failures with object context. If the legacy safety copy fails in mode 3, operators have no log message identifying the kind/name/error to reconcile the divergence; only an aggregate metric counter changes. Each goroutine should log the returned error (without relying on the possibly-cancelled request logger).

Mode 3 tests never wait for or verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example Create at lines 30-32 and Update at lines 313-315) but return/assert immediately after the dual-writer call and never synchronize with the goroutine or call AssertCalled/AssertExpectations for the legacy mock. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is removed, cancelled, or never executes, and leaked goroutines can instead race with later tests using the shared mock/example objects. Tests need a synchronization/wait mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was invoked (and that failures are handled).

Mode 3 integration test synchronously asserts legacy visibility after async writes

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes through the k8s API and immediately checks the legacy playlist API (for example the legacy list/get checks inside doPlaylistTests). Because mode 3 now performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines, there is no happens-before guarantee that the legacy row exists when those assertions run. This makes the new file/unified-storage mode 3 integration cases flaky and can also hide eventual-consistency behaviour that needs polling with a timeout instead of immediate equality assertions.

false_positives.candidate:

I18n.translate only loads config.locale before consulting the LRU cache, not the fallback locales configured in config/initializers/i18n.rb. If a no-argument translation is first looked up when its fallback locale (site default or :en) has not been loaded, translate_no_cache returns a 'translation missing' string and lines 71-76 freeze and cache it under the current locale. Loading the fallback locale later does not invalidate @cache, so the missing-translation string keeps being served until LRU eviction or reload, defeating the fallback feature.

In those contexts I18n.translate loads only the current locale, so keys missing from that locale but present in the site-default or English files return 'translation missing' instead of falling back, making the feature inconsistent between requests and jobs/mailers.

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but overrides [] to ignore anything stored in the hash and always synthesize a value. Every fallback lookup queries SiteSetting and crashes if it is unset

There is no coverage that a missing key in the user locale resolves to the site-default then English text, that duplicate locales (user == default == :en) are de-duplicated, or that fallback files are loaded in non-controller contexts, so the cache-poisoning and jobs/mailers gaps above can regress undetected.

The endpoint should clamp limit to a sane range (e.g. 1..some max) and offset to >= 0.

Public group members page silently truncates membership to the first 50 users

findMembers now always requests the default limit of 50 members, and GroupsController#members now applies that limit to all groups (previously non-automatic groups returned their full member list and automatic groups defaulted to 200). The public template discourse/templates/group/members.hbs renders `members` with no pagination controls, unlike the new admin UI, so for any group with more than 50 members the remaining members are unreachable from the public members page.

The client's Group.asJSON() sends alias_level and the group form shows the alias-level combo-box even for a not-yet-saved group, but Admin::GroupsController#create only assigns name and visible before saving. Any alias level chosen while creating a group is silently lost and the group is created with the default alias_level; only editing and re-saving afterwards sets it. findMembers clamps offset to user_count, landing on an empty page after the last member of a page is removed

The requested offset is clamped with Math.min(user_count, offset). Removing the sole member shown on the last page (e.g. offset 50 of 51 members) triggers removeMember -> findMembers while user_count is still the stale 51, so offset 50 is requested even though only 50 members remain, and the server returns an empty page with total 50. Combined with the inflated totalPages, the admin is left staring at an empty page instead of being moved back to the previous page; the clamp should be based on the last valid page start, not user_count.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write save during validation, double-counting and losing concurrent updates

should_block? is called from EmailValidator during User validation, yet it mutates and saves the BlockedEmail record (`match_count += 1; last_match_at = ...; record.save`). Validation is not a single occurrence: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which re-validates, so one signup attempt increments match_count at least twice, and any other `valid?` check also permanently increments it even if the user is never saved. The read-modify-write is also not atomic, so concurrent attempts reading the same match_count overwrite each other and lose counts. Use an atomic increment (e.g. update_counters/increment_counter with a separate last_match_at update) and avoid counting purely on validation, or at minimum make the update atomic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the should-block check has side effects: it updates match statistics during what should be a read or validation operation, and this causes race conditions under concurrency. The method name differs slightly, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

PostgreSQL string equality is case-sensitive, so a blocked address such as `bad@spam.com` is bypassed by registering as `Bad@Spam.com`, `BAD@spam.com`, etc., defeating the block list this PR introduces. Normalize (downcase/strip) on both BlockedEmail save and in should_block?/the validator lookup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same flaw: the lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? is case-sensitive, so someone can get past a blocked address by registering with a different capitalization of it.

false_positives.candidate:
